title: macOS 27.3 includes new privacy controls for Full Disk Access and more
snippet: Last month, Apple announced its plans to tighten macOS privacy controls around Full Disk Access amid the rise of “increasingly capable and autonomous” AI agents. With today’s new macOS 27.3 beta, Apple is implementing several changes as part of this. more…
fullText:
Last month, Apple announced its plans to tighten macOS privacy controls around Full Disk Access amid the rise of “increasingly capable and autonomous” AI agents.

With today’s new macOS 27.3 beta, Apple is implementing several changes as part of this.

In a post on its developer website last month, Apple said some developers are “using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems.” As such, it said that it would “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”

What’s changing in macOS 27.3

In macOS 27.2, “Device Control and Data Access” is a unified toggle in System Settings, where Apple says that apps with that level of access can “view and send email, edit contacts and photos, monitor your keyboard, track websites, record your screen, control any app on your Mac, and more.”

In macOS 27.3, Apple is splitting “Device Control and Data Access” into two categories:

Accessibility: Intended specifically for assistive technologies, with permissions handled through an entitlement process.

System and App Protection Override: A new category for apps that need to bypass certain macOS protections to control other apps or perform automated tasks.

For the latter, users will be able to specify which apps an automation tool can access rather than granting it unrestricted control. For instance, you could give an app access to the Mail app, but not Messages.

macOS 27.3 also adds an option for users to require an app to request permission every time it requires access, rather than granting it access indefinitely. 

Apple is also introducing a new menu bar indicator that will provide additional transparency when an app is controlling another app with System and App Protection Override. This is designed to let users know when an automation tool is interacting with apps and information in the background.

Full Disk Access isn’t going away

Crucially, Apple isn’t removing the ability to give an app Full Disk Access. If you deem it necessary, you can still give an app Full Disk Access. However, Apple is redesigning the approval process to make the implications of that decision more obvious.

macOS 27.3 will display a more detailed explanation about the protections being bypassed and the types of personal information that could be exposed.

Users can also choose to grant an app access to specific folders instead of their entire Mac. For example, an app that only needs to work with files in a particular folder won’t get unrestricted access to everything else.

Any app you’ve already given Full Disk Access will still have that access. Previously granted permissions will remain in effect, and those apps will continue functioning as they do today without any approval required.

For developers

Apple says the underlying APIs aren’t changing, but developers will need to update their apps to account for situations where users grant limited access rather than unrestricted permissions.

Finally, Apple says developers of backup apps and assistive technologies can request entitlements that allow them to maintain the same experience for new installations as before macOS 27.3. Apple has already identified popular apps that rely on these permissions, and those apps will continue working as expected without requiring an entitlement.

title: Apple’s Siri AI smart glasses are reportedly launching next year, here’s what to expect
snippet: Apple’s long awaited smart glasses, akin to Meta Ray-Bans but tailored to Siri AI and the Apple ecosystem, are almost here. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the product should be introduced at the next WWDC, and they should be on the market by the end of the year. Here’s what to expect. more…
fullText:
Apple’s long awaited smart glasses, akin to Meta Ray-Bans but tailored to Siri AI and the Apple ecosystem, are almost here. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the product should be introduced at the next WWDC, and they should be on the market by the end of the year. Here’s what to expect.

First and foremost, Apple wants to rely on its deep app ecosystem to give its glasses a boost. While companies like Meta are undeniably leading in the agentic AI assistant game, the third party app integration just isn’t quite there.

Starting with iOS 27.3 beta, Apple is finally laying the groundwork for proper third party app integration within Siri, rather than just Siri Shortcuts. By the time the glasses release at the end of next year, there should be a plethora of third-party integrations to utilize.

That said, the glasses themselves won’t run apps directly. Everything will rely on a nearby iPhone, per Gurman. The glasses will still have Wi-Fi for apps to function if an iPhone isn’t nearby, but these will largely serve as an iPhone accessory.

According to the report, Apple’s glasses will likely be slightly thinner than a pair of Meta Ray-Bans:

In terms of industrial design, internal prototypes are slightly thinner than Meta’s second-generation Ray-Ban glasses. At least on some test units, the cameras are housed in oval-shaped openings that sit flush with the frame — rather than protruding from it. There’s also a light on the front that shows when the glasses are in use or charging. Apple has been experimenting with other features on the front of the glasses related to privacy.

Lastly, a big focus of these glasses is the audio quality. According to Bloomberg, engineers are describing the audio quality as “industry-leading.”

title: The UGREEN HomeAgent is a ‘local-first’ way to make your smart home even smarter
snippet: Smart home tech often relies solely on cloud connections and pricey AI subscriptions, but UGREEN is delivering a local-first solution in its new HomeAgent collection, delivering cameras, speakers, and more that bring the bulk of the functionality and processing directly to your home. more…
fullText:
Smart home tech often relies solely on cloud connections and pricey AI subscriptions, but UGREEN is delivering a local-first solution in its new HomeAgent collection, delivering cameras, speakers, and more that bring the bulk of the functionality and processing directly to your home.

The UGREEN AIoT – AI of Things – ecosystem is built around pairing hardware to a central hub that acts as your home’s brain. The HomeAgent HA100 and Pro are that “brain,” pairing to smart home gear such as lights, speakers, and cameras to not only store recordings, but process the data locally.

At the core of the experience is UGREEN’s Uliya AI assistant, which you can talk to directly through HomeAgent HA100 or through a connected Smart Speaker for Uliya. The assistant can handle simple tasks like controlling lights or playing music, of course, but can do a lot more with video recordings. You can ask questions such as “is there a package outside” or “where is my dog” and Uliya will be able to parse through camera recordings to find the answer rather than forcing you to have to scroll through timelines.

That’s all powered by the HomeAgent HA100. It can also acts as network storage for photos, household files, and more, all of which can be used as context for the local AI system – and there’s no monthly fee to store or access it.

	

UGREEN’s hardware lineup around the HomeAgent centerpieces includes cameras such as the SynCare cameras. These deliver the local recording capabilities that are so central to the system. SynCare OD800 Pro is a triple-lens outdoor camera with solar power and a built-in battery, while the OD600 Pro delivers the same powerful camera setup with power-over-ethernet. These have an 8MP primary camera and dual 5MP cameras with pan-tilt-zoom capabilities. They can zoom in up to 9x, feature motion tracking and a built-in spotlight, as well as color night vision and IP66 dust/water protection.

Meanwhile, the SynCare Indoor Cam ID500 Pro is a pan-tilt-zoom camera meant to be used inside to capture events in an entire room. It features 4K imaging, 360-degree pan and 160-degree vertical tilt while supporting up to 8x digital zoom, motion tracking, and even baby-cry detection. It also has a physical shutter for your privacy.

There are also two smart frames, the UGREEN Gallery E-Paper Smart Frame mounts on the wall to display photos and artwork, while the UGREEN Gallery LCD Smart Frame can sit on a table or hang on the wall, showing photos and videos, while also integrating with the rest of your smart home’s functions.

UGREEN has its own smart speaker for the system, and you can also integrate select Matter hardware as well, including smart lighting, robot vacuums and other smart home devices.

The UGREEN HomeAgent ecosystem will start at $799 for a limited time when its Kickstarter campaign launches on April 13, 2027, with upgraded packages that drastically increase AI processing power, storage, and the types of devices you can connect to the system.

You can reserve your UGREEN HomeAgent today to lock in early bird pricing. Reservations are open from September 4, 2026, through April 12, 2027, and deposits can be canceled for a refund any time before the campaign ends. Shipping will begin in late June 2027, with different phases for different products.

title: Apple Launches New App to Study How People Use AI for Health
snippet: This is everything you need to know about the research study’s eligibility, requirements and privacy.
fullText:
Since 2019, when Apple first launched its Research app, the company has partnered with medical universities and institutions to run a range of health studies on hearing, heart health and movement, women’s health and, most recently, the Apple Health Study, which covers a wide variety of health areas. 

On Sunday, Apple launched its latest study, and it comes with its own app: the Apple Health AI Study. 

During a press briefing, Apple said the study aims to understand how people interact with conversational health AI tools. To do so, it will examine comprehension, response quality, the drivers of user trust and everyday health actions.

			

More from CNET

The goal? To inform the responsible design of health AI experiences for both Apple and the industry and to explore how health AI might help people prepare for doctor’s visits. Key questions the study aims to address include: Do users understand the information provided by health AI? Do they trust it? Is it helpful?

This is particularly relevant considering that one in three US adults use AI chatbots for health information. 

Study data will not be used to train AI models, but it may inform Apple’s feature development.

Apple’s study partner

To facilitate the study, Apple is partnering with OpenEvidence, an AI platform designed specifically for doctors. It generates answers using medical information from these partners: The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, National Comprehensive Cancer Network, Nature and Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 

The Apple Health AI Usage Study combines an Apple-designed research experience with OpenEvidence’s AI technology. Apple

In the dedicated app, study participants can ask the AI their text-based health questions and then see answers with linked, peer-reviewed clinical citations. They can also choose to share their HealthKit data, including sleep, lab results, activity and resting heart rate, for more personalized answers. 

HealthKit is Apple’s hub for health and fitness data collected on the iPhone and Apple Watch. 

Who’s eligible?

The Apple Health AI Usage Study is open to 200,000 participants. You must be in the US and age 21 or older to participate. An Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone (iPhone 15 Pro or later) running iOS 26 or later is also required.

Why an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone? According to Apple, the study app requires the processing capabilities of those iPhones, and it uses on-device Apple Foundation Models that are part of Apple Intelligence. These models provide access to any large language model. For example, as part of the study, these models are used to classify question categories. 

What’s required?

Each participant is asked to participate for up to 12 months. During this time, they can ask questions about general health, specific symptoms, recovery from a procedure and their own uploaded health data, as examples. 

After each response, participants will rate the answer and describe what went well and what could be improved. Apple

In addition to a baseline survey, participants will receive monthly surveys and additional surveys specific to preparing for doctor’s visits.

Participants will also be prompted to check in with the app. For instance, if you have a paired Apple Watch, you will receive notifications to check in, along with suggested topics to explore. 

If there is a complete lack of participation, a participant may potentially be removed from the study. 

After the doctor’s visit, there will be surveys to see how things went and whether the tools provided to prepare for the visit were helpful. Apple

Study privacy

After downloading the Apple Health AI Study app, participants must complete a mandatory onboarding process that includes informed consent. They will also be asked to share their demographic information, such as race, age and education level, which will be used to explore how these factors may affect their preferences and communication needs. Then, they can start asking the AI questions. 

The iPhone first processes questions using tools designed to remove details that could identify participants. They then go to a secure cloud-based study environment managed by a third-party study support contractor called UST Global, where queries are delinked from individual participant IDs and screened using tools designed to further remove any remaining personal details. Lastly, this info is sent to OpenEvidence, where answers are generated using supporting reference materials. 

OpenEvidence will delete both question and response data within 24 hours.

A small group of Apple researchers will have access to coded versions of survey responses, separated from personally identifiable information, summaries of conversations and categories of the most common conversation types. 

Within the study app, there are also safety guardrails that detect concerning questions and respond by suggesting that a participant follow up with a provider or other resources if needed. 

There is no live monitoring, and study staff won’t contact participants if any questions related to self-harm are asked.

It’s also up to the participant whether they share any HealthKit metrics. They will first have to choose to upload their clinical health records to Apple’s Health app, and then separately choose to share those records from the Health app to the new Apple Health AI Study app. 

Availability

The Apple Health AI Study app is now available in the App Store. As of now, there is no set publication date for the study.

title: OpenAI will embed safety researchers to investigate AI subversion
snippet: OpenAI will embed six Apollo Research evaluators to investigate whether its AI models engage in subversive behavior, but restrictions on access and disclosure raise questions about their independence.
fullText:
OpenAI will embed safety evaluators from Apollo Research, Goodfire, METR, and Transluce in its organization as part of a pilot, OpenAI said Monday. The news follows a series of safety incidents, including one in which an OpenAI agent swarm broke out of its sandbox and hacked into Hugging Face during cybersecurity testing. Many AI safety researchers, including from Apollo, have argued such an event might have been avoided if outside evaluators had been embedded within OpenAI to monitor its safety testing.

OpenAI said the efforts support its commitments to rely on independent assessments of safety controls under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence. The pilots will begin at different points, with Apollo’s beginning this week, according to OpenAI. 

The idea of embedding evaluators into frontier AI labs first came from Anthropic, which last month started to give METR researchers employee-level access to its systems. Until recently, AI companies have only brought in outside reviewers to test models after post-training and shortly before public release. Evaluators say this is insufficient because it doesn’t allow them to test for misaligned behaviors like scheming during training or to monitor internal deployment use cases that could still pose a threat. 

The work with each third-party firm differs in scope. The pilot with OpenAI and Apollo will focus on investigating whether models attempt to subvert their own or their successors’ alignment or control mechanisms. In other words, they’ll be on the lookout for whether AI models try to undermine the safety rules and safeguards designed to keep them, or future versions of themselves, under human control. OpenAI recently published findings that while training GPT-5.6 Sol, it began leaving instructions for future versions of itself telling them to conceal mistakes and misaligned behavior from the user. 

Per Apollo, the pilot will examine whether training incentivizes subversion; whether evaluations can elicit subversion; whether subversion occurs during internal deployment; and whether reasoning relevant to subversion would be detectable. These risks are becoming increasingly important to monitor as AI models grow more capable of acting autonomously and deceiving humans. Apollo’s previous research with OpenAI found that models can behave differently when they know they’re being tested and tend to prioritize what evaluators want to see over users’ actual institutions. 

Goodfire will embed researchers who specialize in understanding how AI models work internally. Using its interpretability platform, the firm will help OpenAI monitor training runs, fix undesired behavior, and improve alignment, per the company. Goodfire says it will publish findings, though its primary audience will be OpenAI’s own researchers.

With METR, OpenAI plans to perform two evaluations: one that looks for unintended or dangerous behavior in the model itself, including problems OpenAI’s own tests might have missed, and another that tests whether OpenAI’s systems are capable of catching that behavior. For the first evaluation, METR will largely decide for itself what to investigate and how to test the model. OpenAI and METR have not yet come to a decision on the scope of the second assessment, according to OpenAI.

Transluce, meanwhile, will examine whether OpenAI’s post-training safety evaluations themselves are good enough. The organizations also planning to test in 2027 how OpenAI uses its safety tests to decide whether a model is safe enough to release. 

At a time when the independence of third-party evaluations is under scrutiny, it’s worth noting that Apollo and Goodfire are both receiving financial compensation for their evaluations. METR and Transluce aren’t, but they may accept compute or API credits. 

Apollo, which published the most detailed account of its agreement with OpenAI, offers a closer look at the scope and limitations of these evaluations. 

Many in the AI safety community have warned that AI labs might try to stymy evaluators’ independence, especially if outsiders find unflattering evidence that labs would rather keep hidden. Apollo says an essential part of the pilot is OpenAI’s agreement that the firm can publicly explain the conditions and limitations of its work.

Still, there are areas where Apollo believes its access to OpenAI’s systems is lacking. For a truly independent evaluation of the company’s AI models, Apollo says it needs true employee-level access to OpenAI’s systems, including “all data, records and documentation relevant to their assessment even if a developer was trying to hide unfavorable information.” Getting access to all data, including training data and evaluation logs which companies are loathe to show to outsiders, is important for, say, checking a company’s claims about how a model performed or determining when certain concerning behavior emerged. 

In previous coverage, John Steidley, chief of staff at Palisade Research, told TechCrunch that it’s important to see this data in order to assess whether a model was trained to perform well on a “shutdown resistance benchmark.” 

In OpenAI’s first pilot, the AI lab is providing Apollo with access to only the information required to assess whether the models engage in subversion attempts. This includes “relevant training code and datasets, reinforcement-learning rollouts with available reasoning traces and rewards, and the ability to query intermediate model checkpoints.”

The scope of access will be limited to “only the agreed claims and only for the specific models and time periods agreed for the assessment,” Apollo says. OpenAI still reserves the right to withhold certain information within that scope if it deems it necessary because of technical infeasibility, security risks, or IP protection. The company agreed not to withhold information simply because it is unfavorable. 

Apollo also won’t get access to all OpenAI staffers, instead being limited to “only authorized staff,” which are participants that the AI lab selects, though Apollo can suggest certain individuals. Crucially, if an OpenAI employee outside this group raises confidential information within the scope of Apollo’s research, the firm cannot follow up and will need to cease communication and route followup through OpenAI.

That condition is significant. It comes in the wake of OpenAI firing three researchers for allegedly sharing confidential information with safety evaluation firm METR — which performed the Hugging Face incident post-mortem alongside Redwood. 

The pilot will also be limited in how much researchers can disclose. While Apollo will be allowed to publish independent conclusions of its findings, OpenAI will be able to limit evidence available to substantiate them publicly, which could make it hard for outsiders to independently assess the findings. Apollo has pushed back against this limitation, saying it believes researchers should be allowed to disclose the findings of the evaluation “to an appropriate outside audience even if the developer was trying to prevent the disclosure of unfavorable findings.”

That said, while the public cannot see the full supporting evidence, OpenAI says its Safety and Security Committee, which oversees safety on behalf of the OpenAI Foundation’s board, will get to review unredacted assessment reports and can communicate privately with evaluators. 

While OpenAI is not granting all of Apollo’s conditions for a truly independent evaluation, the firm says the pilot is “an ambitious first step towards deeper access and disclosure rights,” and that it is working towards running full embedded evaluations with multiple AI developers in the future.

This article has been updated to include pilots with METR, Goodfire, and Transluce, as well as with information from OpenAI.

title: Apple provides a safe way to ask an AI questions about your health
snippet: A growing number of people are asking AI chatbots about their health issues, raising two major concerns: safety and privacy. Apple is now offering a safer way to do this through an Apple Health AI Usage Study. This is actually one of Apple’s research studies, but those volunteering to take part in it will be able to ask health questions – with three key assurances not guaranteed by other AI chatbots … more…
fullText:
A growing number of people are asking AI chatbots about their health issues, raising two major concerns: safety and privacy. Apple is now offering a safer way to do this through an Apple Health AI Usage Study.

This is actually one of Apple’s research studies, but those volunteering to take part in it will be able to ask health questions – with three key assurances not guaranteed by other AI chatbots …

Apple Health AI Usage Study

Apple launched its Research app back in 2019 with the goal of allowing customers to help universities and medical institutions with health studies. You typically agree to share certain anonymized information from the Apple Health app in order to provide data that can advance medical research. You may also be asked to complete questionnaires.

The Apple Health AI Usage Study is one of these, but it works in a somewhat different way. You’ll still be invited to share some of your health data, but will also be able to ask an AI system questions about your health.

Three key assurances

When you ask health questions of a typical AI chatbot, you don’t know how reliable those answers may be or what will happen to your data. Apple study offers three assurances:

Authoritative sources

Not used for AI training

No retention of questions or answers

Authoritative sources

Apple says that answers will be generated by the same platform used by healthcare professionals.

The study is conducted in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a leading clinical AI platform widely used by healthcare professionals that generates answers using medical information from established sources such as The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, and Nature. 

The answers provided to you will include links to peer-reviewed clinical citations.

Your data won’t be used for AI training

As you’d expect from Apple, there are strong privacy protections, including the assurance that your data will not be used to train AI models.

The study is designed from the ground up with privacy protections, transparency, and clinical guardrails, and study data will not be used to train AI models. Participants retain control over whether to share any HealthKit metrics or survey responses, and Apple has implemented security measures to protect the study data it maintains, as well as the confidentiality of participants’ information.

No retention of questions or answers

CNET reports on Apple’s assurance that none of your chats will be retained.

OpenEvidence will delete both question and response data within 24 hours. A small group of Apple researchers will have access to coded versions of survey responses, separated from personally identifiable information, summaries of conversations and categories of the most common conversation types.

How to get access

Access to the study is currently limited to users in the US by downloading the app. If you try it, please do share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Apple launches new app to study how people use AI for health
snippet: Apple's new app for a study will answer everyday medical questions
fullText:
Big AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic have made their bets on offering chatbots that can answer health-related queries with specialized features. Apple is debuting a new study to understand how people use AI for health. But it isn’t quite following other AI startups just yet; it wants to study how clinically grounded answers can help people.

The iPhone maker is partnering with healthcare-focused AI company OpenEvidence to launch a new study app. Apple is inviting users in the U.S. over 21, using iPhone 15 or later, and running iOS 26 or later, with Apple Intelligence enabled. The company is aiming to run this study with up to 200,000 participants for more than 12 months.

The new app will allow users to ask health-related questions, as they do with ChatGPT or Claude, with answers grounded in clinical data, from sources including The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, and Nature. Apple said that the app will try to give simplified answers to everyday medical questions. Users can rate those answers and provide feedback about the responses; they’ll also be asked to participate in monthly surveys.

Image Credits: AppleImage Credits:Apple

Participants can share data from HealthKit such as resting heart rate, activity, sleep, or lab results to get more personalized and pointed suggestions from the app. The company said the app can also help prepare participants better for a doctor’s visit, and it will guide users to specific providers for answers related to concerning medical issues.

Apple specified that the data will be anonymized before sending it to a secure third-party cloud provider, and it won’t be used to train any kind of AI models. The company said that OpenEvidence deletes the query and response data after 24 hours.

Image Credits: AppleImage Credits:Apple

“At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life,” Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, said in a statement, adding, “Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey.”

The app is available to download starting today for U.S. users. It’s not clear if Apple wants to release AI-powered answering to its Health app or Siri yet. The potential is huge — earlier this year, OpenAI said users were asking over 300 million health-related queries each week.

title: Here’s how Google’s Android XR glasses are handling the camera & privacy
snippet: Google’s Intelligent Eyewear push with the first Android XR glasses from Warby Parker and Gentle Monster are forced into an unfortunate uphill battle. The “perv glasses” stigma is very real because, frankly, early movers in this category didn’t respect privacy. Here’s how Android XR and Gemini are handling the camera and privacy on “Intelligent Eyewear,” and why I think Google has struck a near-perfect balance. more…
fullText:
Google’s Intelligent Eyewear push with the first Android XR glasses from Warby Parker and Gentle Monster are forced into an unfortunate uphill battle. The “perv glasses” stigma is very real because, frankly, early movers in this category didn’t respect privacy. Here’s how Android XR and Gemini are handling the camera and privacy on “Intelligent Eyewear,” and why I think Google has struck a near-perfect balance.

To quickly summarize the problem at hand (and name names), Meta’s smart glasses developed a reputation of being abused by bad actors who would disable the visible privacy LED (which Meta only recently fixed) or use these glasses in tasteless ways. Combine that with improper handling of recordings on Meta’s part and it’s a recipe for distrust and an earned social stigma. It’s not like Google is a simple bystander here, either. The original Google Glass project was met with the “Glasshole” stigma, and it’s something that Google has clearly learned a lot of lessons from.

It’s a shame, because a camera in smart glasses serves such a functional role, both for the user in just capturing pictures and for the AI assistant built into the experience. I recently talked about how the camera was my favorite part of smart glasses in an issue of our 9to5Google Weekender newsletter, but how it just feels a bit wrong now.

Anyway, with that context in mind, let’s look at how Google is handling this touchy subject.

	

It starts with the outward-facing light on every part of Android XR glasses, which works similarly to the privacy LED on Meta’s glasses. The key distinction here is this is a “recording light” on Android XR glasses. It turns on whenever the glasses are capturing content that can be viewed later in some form or fashion by the user. So if you’re taking a picture or recording a video, it lights up. If you’re just using Gemini for context, the light doesn’t activate. That’s because any camera captures being used for Gemini are deleted immediately after use. They won’t show up in your Gemini chat logs and that’s not a choice for the user – these images are purged immediately after they’ve been used so that you as the user nor Google can use them. That includes Google not using visuals from Gemini captures for AI training or advertising. Users also have control over what apps on Android XR glasses can use the camera.

The camera on a pair of Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear glasses

Importantly, the light on each pair of Android XR glasses is also designed to avoid any tampering. Android XR glasses automatically perform a system check to ensure the light is working on a regular basis – you might catch the light blinking in white and blue while charging which is a part of the system check ensuring the hardware is fully functional. If the light is found not to be working, the camera is disabled.

One of the pieces of this package that really caught my attention is how Google is handling the privacy of those around you. When your Intelligent Eyewear glasses send a photo to Gemini, your phone automatically redacts faces from the image before it’s sent to Gemini. This happens locally on the phone, essentially as a part of the glasses app. Similarly, voice data sent to Gemini filters out other voices besides your own. The voice filtering bit is just one way in which Google is doing some impressive things with the microphones here, with another example being that the live translation feature works in a 60-degree “cone” in front of you, filtering out other voices in the space.

Continuing on with how the camera interacts with Gemini, Google explained in a conversation with 9to5Google that Gemini is tuned not to use the camera in cases where it’s not obvious that the user wants the camera to be active. An interaction such as “what painting is this” would very clearly imply that the user wants the glasses to view the scene in front of them and identify the art piece, where “how much money is on the table,” Google explained, would ask for a follow-up before using the camera seeing as it’s not obvious that the user expects the camera to be used in that sort of phrase.

Another way in which Android XR glasses will avoid the recording stigma is with their limits. Google is limiting Intelligent Eyewear video recording to 90-second sessions. While that does limit what the user can do, Google said that most recordings fell within that window anyway. Meta, by comparison, offers recordings up to 5 minutes. 

Beyond just the glasses app and Gemini, Google says it is making other efforts across its ecosystem to protect against and deter misuse of the camera on Android XR glasses, including:

Responsible use requirements: Before using intelligent eyewear, users must agree not to record others without permission, not to record in sensitive places, and not to cover the recording indicator light. Not following these requirements is a violation of the Google Terms of Service, and a user’s ability to use the glasses may be disabled.

Google Shopping and Google Ads: Policies ban the sale and advertising of stickers or accessories designed to hide recording lights.

Google Play: Policies prohibit apps from using the camera for social live-streaming or real-time facial identification, and from changing the behavior of the outer indicator light.

YouTube: Policies prohibit content that depicts things like harassment and unwanted sexualization. Any video uploaded to YouTube — whether it’s recorded on a phone, a camera, or glasses — has to follow these policies, and videos that don’t are removed.

Account restrictions: Activating an intelligent eyewear device requires an 18+ Google account.

9to5Google’s Take

For the most part, Google’s efforts around privacy on Android XR glasses aren’t groundbreaking. This is how it should work. But seeing as the bar is exceptionally low thanks to a rough start from competitors, I found myself reassured and even a bit impressed by the messaging here – a clear explanation of the indicator light and the automatic on-device face redaction and deletion of Gemini imagery both go a long way.

Google’s sentiment around privacy on glasses is pretty nearly summed up by a sentence in its privacy post today: “…when technology can see the world around you, it has a responsibility to the people around you, too.” 

What do you think?

title: Jordan Belfort’s new AI voice startup, Tone, wants to sell like the ‘Wolf of Wall Street’
snippet: Belfort claims his AI sales voice can already close deals almost as well as the best human salespeople, and he thinks it will catch up in a year.
fullText:
Years ago, as questions mounted about WeWork’s soaring valuation, I sat down with co-founder Adam Neumann. We were negotiating a stage interview, and he asked to meet me twice in the weeks leading up to it, once at a WeWork in San Francisco and again at his office in New York. 

I knew full well that the numbers that SoftBank in particular had assigned to WeWork made little sense, but I came away understanding why investors wanted to throw in their lot with him.

It’s similarly easy to understand why people are enchanted by Jordan Belfort, the self-proclaimed “Wolf of Wall Street.” Belfort famously pleaded guilty in 1999 to securities fraud and money laundering tied to Stratton Oakmont, the Long Island brokerage where salespeople pushed penny stocks in pump-and-dump schemes while Belfort acquired a Southampton mansion, a 167-foot yacht, and at least one helicopter. (He destroyed the latter two while high on Quaaludes and cocaine, as depicted in Martin Scorsese’s famous adaptation of Belfort’s autobiography, “The Wolf of Wall Street.”)

You might think someone who spent 22 months in prison and was ordered to pay $110.4 million in restitution to 1,513 victims wouldn’t get another shake. The victims ultimately received “far less” than they were owed, TMZ reported in July, noting that Belfort completed his court-ordered restitution obligations in late April of this year.

But Belfort, whose energy has a galvanizing quality, keeps resurfacing, including in recent years as a Miami-based sales consultant and one-time host of crypto workshops at his Miami Beach home. (A New York Times reporter attended a weekend workshop several years ago where the price of admission was one bitcoin or its equivalent value at the time of $40,000.)

Now, he is moving into the intersection of what he knows best — sales — and the hottest trend on the planet, AI, building out a voice-based AI platform. The secret sauce is that it imbues its voices with the kind of tonality that wins deals, he says, for example, by phrasing declarative statements as questions (which “builds engagement”) and even whispering at times (which “implies scarcity of information”).

Belfort says the platform, called Tone, is already being used by companies that have more sales leads than their human teams can handle. Now, in a move that could also help expand its training data, Tone is launching a self-service platform for content creators and authors who want to turn their books into “expressive AI-generated narration.” Users can select from Tone’s AI voices or, as a voice-cloning feature rolls out, create a clone of their own voice.

It’s easy to argue the market is already saturated with AI voice startups and technologies, and Tone comes with added risk:  Belfort’s co-founder in the business is longtime investor Shervin Pishevar, who has a controversial past of his own. We also can’t independently verify that the technology works as described (neither co-founder is an engineer).

But if my time with Neumann taught me anything, it’s that doubts about the numbers rarely get in the way of a good pitch. When Belfort looks for investors to back him in this new venture, finding believers won’t be too hard.

Here is part of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.

What have you built?

It’s a very unique way of going about building a voice, and it stems from a system of influence and persuasion I’ve been teaching since the late 1980s. It’s not just what you say, but how you say it. When you’re not in person, body language collapses into tonality. There are about 15 very powerful tonalities that people use all the time. The phrase I invented for this was “goal-oriented communication.” If I’m trying to be perceived as an expert, I apply tonality strategically.

Is this effectively trained on you?

It started that way. As a non-engineer, I went to first principles: How would I teach a human to do this? One tonality at a time. I have 30 years of super high-quality data , and I started teaching the model. It was a breakthrough moment, because it not only sounded exactly like me, it had nailed the tonality. Then I taught it a second one, and then how to link them. The key to all of this is data. Even the littlest bit of corrupt data dramatically negates the progress you’ve made.

How did you and Shervin Pishevar come together?

Shervin and I have been personal friends for a long time, and we were out for dinner one night. I had been pitched by an AI company that said it had an AI that could do selling. I listened to it. It was awful. But it put the idea in my head. I thought I was just going to teach models how to sell, but I couldn’t find a voice that was good enough. Necessity is the mother of invention, so we built our own.

Who are your customers, and how do they use it?

We have law firms and health insurance companies. We do a lot in polling and automobiles. It will take you through an entire health insurance sale. It asks qualifying questions, like what type of insurance you want, your budget, your ages. Then it chooses a plan and explains the features and benefits. Our latency is like 600 milliseconds. If the payment is too high, it’ll say it can bring the payment down and explain how to raise your deductible. If you don’t like the plan, it swaps you to a different one. It does literally the whole entire sale.

How does the AI handle a sales call that goes off script? 

It never says “That’s a great question,” unless it really is. I hate that. It’s so ingratiating. In any sale there’s a happy path, how we’d want the perfect conversation to go, and every last word can be mapped out. But people have questions and concerns, and they take you off the straight line. So the trick is a model that can carry that perfect conversation, handle anything thrown at it, answer elegantly and return to the straight line, without breaking rapport and without hallucinating — or, as a salesperson, lying. We’ve trained the model to do that.

Have you generated any revenue from Tone yet? Have you raised funding for it? 

Revenue, probably about a million bucks — $700,000, maybe. We’ve raised friends and family and seed, about $10 million.

I want to address the elephant in the room. You have a fraud conviction. Pishevar has faced misconduct allegations that he denies. Why should a bank or a hospital or a consumer brand trust this product coming from the two of you?

All I can say for myself is that I did make mistakes. It was a very, very long time ago, and I’ve spent the last 20-plus years teaching people all over the world. I’ve been hired by companies all over the world to teach sales and persuasion. If some companies don’t want to work with us, that’s their decision. But I think there would be more than enough that would see the value of what we created. 

What close rate does Tone have versus a typical sales force?

I still don’t think it’s quite as good as a top producer. A top producer in the field would outdo it call for call. I think that will change in the next six months to a year. To make a model respond this quickly, you’re not using frontier models. We’re using our own very small, very light models, so they don’t have quite as much intelligence. I think it will significantly outperform a mediocre closer.

Where is it used most effectively? Low-dollar sales opportunities? I’d think the more money someone is spending, the more human contact they’d demand.

I don’t think it’s about replacing humans. What I see most with customers is that they simply don’t have the human capital available. They could get a lot more leads than they have people to call, or they need coverage at different times of day or in different languages. I think there’s always going to be a need for great human salespeople. I really believe that.

You’re competing with ElevenLabs and Cartesia and a lot of other voice AI companies. Tone is your edge?

I don’t think sounding human is really what this is about. They’ll all sound human in six months or a year. It’s the application of tonality that makes us different: the intelligence behind when it chooses a certain tonality. We have a patent on it. ElevenLabs is a great company, and Cartesia as well, but those voices didn’t work for us.

The FCC ruled in 2024 that AI voices fall under robocall rules under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act. How does outbound sales calling work?

We only call opt-in. You’re not going to use AI to cold call people. We would not allow that. You’d get sued by every TCPA lawyer in the world. It’s either opted-in leads or existing customers. The exception is polling, where there’s an exemption that lets you call private homes without opt-in.

How do you verify consent and prevent impersonation in voice cloning?

We could launch the cloning tomorrow. We didn’t. If you create a clone in our system, you speak into the computer, so we know who is creating it, and that person signs a consent. If someone wants to upload audio, which we don’t recommend, you’d have to match a live voiceprint in real time.

Who created the technology? You’re not an engineer, and Pishevar isn’t, either. I saw a name on the patent, Jordan Anthony Metzner.

No. Our VP of engineering is Ben Sussman. He’s a brilliant engineer. I’m the judge and the jury and the executioner of what sounds perfect. I’ll prototype something in the most obscene way, and my engineers rebuild it from scratch. 

Do you charge per minute, or based on the outcomes customers see?

A combination. For streaming, it’s per minute. The content platform will be monthly subscriptions. And we have some clients where the bulk of our money is made through success.

Is this an independent company or something that belongs inside a larger AI company?

If the right offer came up, and it was substantial enough, and I thought it made sense, who wouldn’t entertain a conversation? But right now my plan is to raise a significant amount. I don’t think we need to own data centers, but we need enough reserve compute. I wouldn’t think I’d be selling it anytime soon, but who knows what the future brings.

Paramount+ released a documentary about you this summer. Did you watch it?

I didn’t. Believe it or not, I don’t watch or read anything about me, good or bad. I never read a comment. When you’re well-known, you have to live by who you are inside. I go by my own internal compass.

title: OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet, enabling ‘dot’ agents to make purchases
snippet: OpenAI is launching ChatGPT Wallet, which it says is “setting a new bar for secure payments by agents.” ChatGPT Wallet works with OpenAI’s “dots” agent feature and includes a partnership with American Express, MasterCard, and Visa. Here’s how it works. more…
fullText:
OpenAI is launching ChatGPT Wallet, which it says is “setting a new bar for secure payments by agents.”

ChatGPT Wallet works with OpenAI’s “dots” agent feature and includes a partnership with American Express, MasterCard, and Visa. Here’s how it works.

ChatGPT Wallet lets your dot agent make purchases on your behalf

OpenAI says ChatGPT Wallet is the “first wallet that lets agents pay without access to users’ actual card details and that requires a security check for every purchase, while also preserving existing card rewards and protections for eligible disputes.”

To start, ChatGPT Wallet is only available to ChatGPT Pro subscribers who are 18 or older in the United States.

“We’re starting with limited availability to ChatGPT Pro users,” OpenAI explains, “so we can learn from real-world use and work with businesses, banks, and payment networks to improve compatibility and reliability.”

The feature won’t work with websites that block agents, however, which has increasingly become an issue online. 

More details below:

Before each purchase, the user reviews the items, total, and selected card, then approves it with a security check such as Face ID or a fingerprint scan. Each approval creates a clear record of the purchase the user authorized the agent to make.

After the user approves, the payment network provides a payment token—a substitute for the user’s actual card details—with a card number, security code, and expiration date. The payment is charged to their selected card without ChatGPT Wallet sharing their actual card details with the business or agent.

You can read more about ChatGPT Wallet and how it works here.

The company emphasizes that payments are secure, card info isn’t shared with your dot or merchants, and that you’re in control of purchases. 

Now your dot can securely complete purchases on your behalf—with your approval.

With ChatGPT Wallet, agents pay without access to your actual card details. Every purchase requires a security check.

title: Audible turns to AI to help users discover audiobooks
snippet: Audible's new AI-generated audio previews summarize a book's themes and what readers liked about it, in addition to playing the narrated sample.
fullText:
Amazon-owned audiobook service Audible is turning to AI to help listeners find their next book. The company on Monday launched a new “audio discovery” feature that provides a brief overview of a book’s themes and a summary of what readers liked about it, as well as commentary from an Audible editor or an author, in addition to playing the narrated sample.

The overview audio itself is generated using AI, and the commentary is pulled from recordings of past Audible interviews, the company says. 

The idea is that this type of expanded introduction to a story could help users decide what to listen to next, particularly when they’re on the go and don’t have time to scroll through comments or reviews.

The feature follows last month’s launch of a handful of AI tools that let users engage more with the story, interact with characters, or catch up with the help of recaps. These features have come as Audible faces new competition in the audiobooks market, namely from Spotify, which introduced audiobook listening hours as part of its paid subscriptions. That service expanded last month to over 180 markets.

Audible’s new feature takes a cue from how Amazon is already using AI to help people shop: On the Amazon storefront, AI can summarize buyers’ product reviews so shoppers can get a quick sense of what people had to say, as well as the pros and cons of a particular item. In Audible’s case, it’s pulling information about what people liked about the book from publicly available reviews.

But such a feature could limit users’ exposure to negative reviews if the AI only pulls information from those that offer positive remarks. (Further testing will be needed to see if this is the case, of course.)

Audible says the overviews will also draw on other publicly available materials, like synopses and metadata.

The feature will initially be available for select English-language titles in the U.S., and will arrive alongside new personalized collections based on users’ listening taste that could help them find other books.

The company’s other recent AI features, Recaps and the interactive “Ask a Question” tool, are also now expanding to more U.S. titles, and will become more broadly available in December. These features will only be available to customers who have purchased a title or who have access to the book as part of their Audible membership, the company said.

“Picking your next listen should feel like getting a tip from a friend,” said Andy Tsao, Audible’s chief product and analytics officer, in a statement. “With audio discovery, you’ll get a quick audio take on why the title might be right for you from our editors, fellow listeners, or even the author. Some of the best listening experiences are those rare finds or hidden gems, and we want to make those great discoveries happen more often and more easily,” he added.

title: Bedrock Energy raises $24M to build more AI-enabled geothermal drill rigs for enterprise buildings
snippet: Geothermal heat pumps could free up significant space on the grid. Bedrock Energy raised $24 million to bring its AI-guided drill rigs to more markets.
fullText:
Dig deep enough, and the temperature of the ground remains steady year round, a fun trivia fact that has the potential to improve efficiency and slash costs for heating and cooling across the country.

Geothermal heat pumps, which use the ground as a heat source in winter and heat sink in summer, have been around for decades, but they’re underutilized. Just a fraction of all buildings in the U.S. use them in part because it’s expensive to drill into the earth. But one startup, Bedrock Energy, says its AI-directed rigs can slash drilling times by up to 80%, significantly reducing costs.

That time savings recently helped Bedrock raise a new $24 million funding round, the startup told TechCrunch. Previously, it raised a $12 million Series A in 2025 and an $8.5 million seed round in 2023.

Bedrock has focused mostly on commercial properties to date, since they benefit from deep, accurate boreholes which maximize the use of their small footprints. But the startup has also been talking with data center developers, Joselyn Lai, co-founder and CEO of Bedrock Energy, told TechCrunch. Some might use it for cooling server racks, but others are interested in the technology’s flat load profile — deploying it on neighboring properties can open up significant capacity on the grid. 

“We had someone in Michigan say, if we could free up a few megawatts, I think we might be able to operate that many months or even a year earlier,” Lai said. “A year of revenue for a data center is very meaningful.”

Bedrock says its modernized approach to shallow geothermal drilling — up to 1,000 feet or so — sets it apart. Most geothermal heat pump drillers use rigs that are similar to those used for water wells. They work fine, but they’re crude instruments.

Instead, Bedrock uses directional drilling techniques borrowed from the oil and gas industry, guiding them using its own models of the subsurface. That combination allows them to optimize drilling and placement, the company says, helping to ensure performance and longevity. Sensors in the boreholes help to refine those models.

The startup currently operates in Utah, Colorado, New York, Alberta, and its home state of Texas, and the new round will help the company expand into New England, New Jersey, the upper Midwest, and additional states in the West, Lai said.

To power that expansion, Bedrock will add more rigs to its fleet to serve customers in those regions. Currently, it has drilled boreholes in nine sites, and it has secured payments from new customers in anticipation of drilling in the next year or two, she added.

Once up and running, a geothermal heat pump requires far less maintenance than traditional HVAC systems. “You only have to install it once and then it works for a very long time, which is very good for infrastructure from a financial perspective,” Lai said.

The new round was led by Clean Energy Ventures and Clearvision Ventures, with participation from GVP Climate, Susquehanna Sustainable Investments, Catalytic Capital for Climate and Health by Temasek Trust, MUUS, Great Wave Ventures, Autodesk Foundation, Titanium Ventures, Energy Impact Partners, Wireframe Ventures, Elemental Impact, and SFV Capital.

But one startup, Bedrock Energy, says its AI-directed rigs can slash drilling times by up to 80%, significantly reducing costs.

title: 15 hotel guests were injured by chlorine poisoning due to Microsoft’s global email outage
snippet: Microsoft's worldwide 365 and Outlook outage had real-world consequences after it cut off email alerts for a German hotel's pool safety system. The German outlet Westdeutscher Rundfunk (WDR) said several people were injured at a Phantasialand hotel on Friday after its email system failed to deliver a safety alert about elevated chlorine levels in the pool, as spotted earlier by NotebookCheck and TechRadar. A machine-translated Facebook post from a German fire department said it responded to a Phantasialand hotel after a "technical malfunction" caused an excessive amount of chlorine to enter a swimming pool, resulting in chlorine gas leaking … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Emma Roth

 

is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Microsoft’s worldwide 365 and Outlook outage had real-world consequences after it cut off email alerts for a German hotel’s pool safety system. The German outlet Westdeutscher Rundfunk (WDR) said several people were injured at a Phantasialand hotel on Friday after its email system failed to deliver a safety alert about elevated chlorine levels in the pool, as spotted earlier by NotebookCheck and TechRadar.

A machine-translated Facebook post from a German fire department said it responded to a Phantasialand hotel after a “technical malfunction” caused an excessive amount of chlorine to enter a swimming pool, resulting in chlorine gas leaking into the surrounding area. As reported by WDR, 15 people were affected by the incident, including four who were transported to the hospital.

Microsoft has since published a post-incident report about the outage, and EVP Charles Lamanna posted an abridged version last night on X. The company says three factors contributed significantly to the incident, including a bug introduced in a previous update in July. This, coupled with a surge in load following an earlier Teams outage and an “unrelated issue” from the previous day that knocked out nearly 14 percent of its server capacity, activated the conditions for the “latent” bug in the July update to rear its head, which “caused requests to build up until servers ultimately stopped responding” during the peak traffic window in the US on Thursday.

The outage lasted from Thursday afternoon and well into Friday morning for many businesses on the East Coast, before Microsoft said service was fully restored on Sunday. “Recovery took longer than usual because as servers returned to service, they were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and became unresponsive again,” Microsoft says. “Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state.” Microsoft adds that it couldn’t “quickly revert the change” because the defect was a latent bug from several months ago.

title: Serena Williams winds down her VC firm, launches new fund, targets $200M
snippet: Serena Williams and longtime business partner Beth Ferreira announced Monday the launch of an early-stage firm called Starfire Ventures.
fullText:
Serena Williams and longtime business partner Beth Ferreira announced Monday the launch of an early-stage firm called Starfire Ventures. 

The firm is seeking to raise a $200 million debut fund to back AI-native companies that are “solving critical, underserved problems for individuals across the experience economy,” including in areas such as fintech and health and wellness, the fund said in a press release announcing its launch. 

This fund is separate from Serena Ventures, which Williams founded in 2022. A rep for Starfire confirmed that Serena Ventures has recently cut its last check, though a team remains to support the existing portfolio. Serena Ventures backed more than 100 companies and raised over $100 million in capital. Ferreira worked as an advisor and general partner at Serena Ventures and has co-invested with Williams since 2015 when they backed MasterClass’ seed round. 

This new firm, Starfire, is a continuation of that business partnership, with Williams saying in the press release that it was “designed to live beyond” them and that the goal remains to broaden “access to capital” and create “opportunities for more people to participate in the ownership and growth of transformative businesses.”

title: FBI says Artex AI open-source hacking tool used to breach networks in ‘under three hours’
snippet: The FBI says that the open-source hacking tool was used in cyberattacks targeting a U.S. IT giant and the South Korean financial industry.
fullText:
The FBI is warning that hackers are relying on autonomous AI hacking tools to launch cyberattacks across the U.S. and globally. The campaigns include a widespread hack of customers of American IT company ConnectWise and across South Korea’s financial industry.

In its latest flash cybersecurity advisory, the FBI says hackers have targeted several industries in recent months, including financial services, government, tech, defense, phone and internet companies, and law firms, using open-source tools like Artex to carry out autonomous-driven cyberattacks.

Artex is one of several open-source AI-powered penetration testing platforms, a category of software built to probe a network’s defenses. Hackers can connect Artex to hosted frontier large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as to open-source models and non-U.S. models. The FBI says Artex intrusions can be “noisy,” meaning they generate reams of traffic and data that may trigger a targeted company’s defensive alerts. But the tools allow hackers to move at speeds that makes it far more harder for human defenders to keep up.

In some cases, Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise “in under three hours.”

The FBI’s warning comes as AI-powered hacks are escalating, particularly by finding easy-to-find security flaws and breaking into companies with relative ease.

Oftentimes, Artex will rely on rapidly scanning a victim’s network to look for signs of weakness, and then exploit simple security bugs, such as weak protections and exposed or stolen passwords to gain a foothold. From there, Artex allows the hacker to spread across the network for databases, mailboxes, and other sensitive information.

The FBI’s advisory noted that Artex has been used in several cyberattacks since the tool’s first public debut in July. Artex was used to hack a number of South Korean financial institutions, blamed in large part on weak cybersecurity defenses and lacking protections, such as multi-factor authentication. The attacks allowed hackers to steal the personal data of at least 68,000 people.

The FBI confirmed earlier findings from Microsoft that hackers also used Artex to break into IT management giant ConnectWise and gain access to the Microsoft 365 cloud environments of at least 2,250 of its customers.

The hackers, who Microsoft says are likely Chinese, used the tool to steal data from affected ConnectWise customers.

A spokesperson for ConnectWise did not respond to a request for comment about the FBI’s claim.

Cybersecurity company Barracuda also disclosed that it was breached as part of an Artex-linked attack by financially motivated criminals, in which the tool found an exposed credential belonging to a third-party service that Barracuda had not revoked when it ended work with the vendor. That access allowed the hackers to access stores of credentials used by Barracuda to collect data from its customers’ systems. Barracuda said it couldn’t rule out access, as its logs were not detailed enough, and chose to “assume the worst” and changed all of its customer credentials.

“Defenders who rely on spotting malicious activity and then responding to it will often arrive after the attacker has finished,” wrote Barracuda’s chief information security officer Arve Kjoelen.

A spokesperson for Barracuda told TechCrunch that the company “directly notified and advised a minority of XDR customers to revoke and recreate integration credentials,” but did not specify how many customers.

After Artex was used in cyberattacks, the tool’s developer made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks. But the FBI says the previous open-source version continues to circulate and remains “widely accessible” for use in cyberattacks.

It’s not only companies and targeted victims that have been compromised as a result of weakened security exploited by AI tools; the tools themselves have been exposed as well, potentially allowing outsiders to access powerful hacking capabilities. Last week, researchers found hundreds of publicly exposed Artex systems online, which had been placed on the internet without a password, likely by mistake or misconfiguration — including the Artex system that was used to target South Korea.

Updated with response from Barracuda.

title: OpenAI releases a new image classifier and ChatGPT warnings to combat CSAM
snippet: ChatGPT will ban an account trying to access CSAM content for 24 hours as a warning
fullText:
OpenAI today announced new tools to combat child sexual abuse material (CSAM) amid growing safety concerns around the use of AI tools. These features include a new image classifier to detect CSAM, warnings and temporary blocks to prevent users from creating or accessing content that sexualizes children, a new guideline for developers, and a set of tools for law enforcement.

The company unveiled a new image classifier that can detect CSAM images, including the ones generated by AI. OpenAI is giving select companies access to its classifier through its API at no cost. The tool looks for visual signs of abuse in images not seen before and assigns a score that can give an indicative direction to reviewers about dealing with CSAM.

OpenAI said that it developed this classifier with the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), and it is working with Tech Coalition and ROOST to share access to the tool. In its early testing with partners, the AI company found that the classifier flags 48% fewer images while finding the same number of abusive images, reducing the work of reviewers. Plus, images flagged by the classifier are twice as likely to be abusive images. 

What’s more, the company is adding new warning screens in ChatGPT to prevent users from accessing material that sexualizes children. ChatGPT will show an alert to users attempting such prompts, direct users towards specialized support to stop harmful behaviour, and also suspend the account for 24 hours as a warning. The app already blocks CSAM content and requests related to it. It said that repeated offences could lead to the account being removed permanently. 

OpenAI noted that it formed the message and guidelines around this behavior with organizations and researchers, including Protect Children, the Lucy Faithfull Foundation, and Joel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, who independently evaluated a trial of deterrent messages.

The company is also publishing guidelines for developers using OpenAI tools to prevent, detect, and help users report CSAM content. It said that in early testing, the guidelines have helped a number of developers adopt child safety tooling and register to report CSAM to NCMEC. OpenAI is also equipping law enforcement dealing with child safety with AI-powered features like dedicated plugins, investigative tools, and complex data analysis, with access managed by program administrators. It is also providing training to investigators along with a field guide on how to use AI.

OpenAI has had several lawsuits against the company blaming its technology for harming users, especially children. Saftey-focused nonprofit Common Sense Media labeled OpenAI’s tech as “unacceptable risk” for teens. Other AI chatbots — specifically Grok — have been used to create nonconsensual sexualized imagery, including of children.

The AI startup had made changes in the last 12 months to its technology including releasing a safety blueprint, updating content guidelines to bar inappropritate content, retuning its model to prevent them from generating harmful content, and releasing a special version of ChatGPT for teens.

title: US tightens AI chip export controls to deter Chinese companies from accessing compute remotely
snippet: Under the interim rule, the U.S. will require firms to get licenses to export AI chips if they may provide compute to China or other restricted countries.
fullText:
The Trump administration on Monday is preparing to roll out new export controls on AI chips and data centers outside the U.S., seeking to prevent companies, especially those in China, from getting past U.S. export controls by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries.

Under the interim rule, the Commerce Department will require companies to get licenses to export, reexport, or transfer AI chips and servers to data centers anywhere in the world if they may provide compute to companies in China or other restricted countries.

The remote-access rules target companies based in the U.S.’s D:5 group of embargoed countries, which includes China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and 18 others.

The U.S. already has rules requiring chip companies to get a license to ship AI chips to companies based in, or owned by any business in, this group of countries. 

“This new control is a logical extension of existing controls,” the interim rule reads. “These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models.” 

The move comes days after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned amid a scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy linked to one of the chipmaker’s customers. The U.S. government has reportedly been wanting to put that customer, Megaspeed, on a special entity list, as it believes the company has been buying thousands of Nvidia chips to provide compute to Chinese businesses to get past existing export-control restrictions.

Reuters reported last week that Chinese AI companies are rushing to secure computing capacity overseas amid fears of tighter restrictions from the U.S.

The rule applies to data centers or any network that can supply over 12 million total processing performance (TPP), an export-control metric the U.S. uses to measure computing power. (Twelve million TPP roughly works out to the max computing power of about 750 Nvidia H100 or H200 chips.) The rule also covers indirect access through go-betweens or brokers, and exporters and data center operators are required to keep an eye on their customers’ ownership structures and activities to ensure they aren’t run by anyone from the D:5 group.

The rule also adds new licensing requirements for chip exports, reexports, or transfer of advanced semiconductors to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil. The Commerce Department said it had included these as they “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion.” For these countries, however, the license requirements will not apply to chips “destined” for companies based in the U.S.

Existing data center operators providing services that fall under this new rule are required to get licenses within 90 days of the rule coming into effect.

Notably, the rule doesn’t apply to commercial recommendation systems, like those used in e-commerce or social media.

The rule also rescinds the Biden admin’s AI Diffusion Rule from January 2025, which sought to impose country-level limits on exports of advanced AI chips, and restrict transfers of certain powerful AI models. That May, the Trump administration said it would throw out that framework, arguing that it added unnecessary restrictions on U.S. companies and the country’s allies.

“By making these changes, this IFR prevents the use of certain SI items in data centers and at a computing power level that can be used for training or running of advanced SI models,” the rule reads. “Access to such computing power can be used to train and run advanced SI models capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten U.S. national security or foreign policy interests.”

title: Freshworks alums raise $53M to take on Salesforce, HubSpot with AI-native CRM
snippet: Dreamteam has signed up more than 100 customers across 13 countries, with some businesses switching from established CRMs.
fullText:
Dreamteam, a startup founded by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million to challenge Salesforce and HubSpot with its AI-native CRM, betting that AI can finally shake up a market where established players have so far proved difficult to dislodge.

The funding comprises seed and Series A rounds, led by Together Fund and Accel respectively, with participation from Premji Invest. The San Francisco-based startup declined to disclose the size of each round or its valuation.

Traditional CRMs depend on salespeople to manually record customer interactions and keep deal information up to date. That often leaves businesses with incomplete or outdated information. Dreamteam aims to eliminate much of that work by automatically capturing context from sources including emails and customer conversations. It also uses AI agents to handle tasks such as follow-ups, meeting preparation, and pipeline monitoring.

Dreamteam co-founder and CEO Anand Venkatraman (pictured above, right) told TechCrunch that he had repeatedly encountered problems with traditional CRM platforms over more than 25 years in enterprise software, including at Salesforce and Freshworks. Salespeople spent considerable time updating records, yet managers still struggled to get a reliable picture of their business. “In all these years, I have never come across an instance where I could click a button and get a forecast from the CRM,” he said.

That experience led Venkatraman to co-found Dreamteam in 2025 with Senthil Kanthaswamy (pictured above, center), who spent more than nine years at Freshworks, most recently as a product leader at Freshservice, and Ramesh Parthasarathy (pictured above, left), who previously worked on AI and platform engineering at Freshworks.

At the heart of Dreamteam’s CRM is what it calls the Company Brain. This acts as virtual memory, pulling together information from emails, meetings, and other customer interactions to build a shared record of customer relationships. Four built-in AI agents use that information to research prospects, draft follow-up emails, flag potential risks to deals, and configure CRM workflows, with sales teams retaining control over what gets sent to customers.

Dreamteam has signed up more than 100 customers across 13 countries in the three months since it began actively selling its product, with most paying for the service, Venkatraman said. The startup has also replaced established CRM platforms at several businesses, including Salesforce at healthcare company DMS Health and HubSpot at other customers.

The advertising sales team at media streaming company Plex also chose Dreamteam over HubSpot and other AI-native CRM alternatives, Venkatraman told TechCrunch. Plex’s co-founder and chief product officer Scott Olechowski said Dreamteam’s ability to integrate with AI tools already used across the company was a “game changer.”

Replacing established CRM platforms at scale may prove more difficult. In a blog post earlier this year, venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) argued that while AI could transform how businesses manage customer relationships, existing CRMs are likely to remain the systems where customer records are stored, with a new generation of AI-powered tools capturing much of the value by working on top of them.

Venkatraman acknowledged that Salesforce and HubSpot are unlikely to disappear anytime soon, but noted that their entrenched positions do not guarantee they will dominate the next generation of CRM software. 

“We see this as an electric-car moment for systems of record,” he said, adding that AI requires a fundamental rethink of how CRMs are built — not simply adding new features to existing platforms.

Kanthaswamy believes startups have a window of two to five years to gain ground before established CRM providers can fully adapt to AI. Rebuilding software around a fundamentally different architecture takes time, he stated, giving newer companies an opportunity to attract customers while incumbents work to overhaul their existing products.

Dreamteam also plans to expand beyond sales into other parts of the customer lifecycle, including onboarding, customer support, and upselling. The startup already has a feature called Magic Apps that allows users to create custom applications and dashboards within the CRM using natural-language instructions, without writing code.

Currently, Dreamteam employs more than 35 people, with its engineering team based in Chennai and its go-to-market operations in the United States. Kanthaswamy said the startup aims to reach eight figures in annual revenue by the end of 2027, though he declined to disclose the startup’s current revenue.
