title: Apple reveals how iCloud+ increases Siri AI and Apple Intelligence usage limits
snippet: iOS 27.3 beta 2 is now available, and Apple is adding the ability for users to unlock higher usage limits for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI via iCloud+. Here’s everything you need to know. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.3 beta 2 is now available, and Apple is adding the ability for users to unlock higher usage limits for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI via iCloud+. Here’s everything you need to know. 

From the start, Apple has said that some Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features have usage limits because “they rely on powerful server models.” The company previously outlined that increased access would be available across most iCloud+ subscription plans, and now we have the full details on how this will work.

Apple says the new system applies to several categories of Apple Intelligence features, including:

Siri AI

Photo tools: Clean Up, Extend, Spatial Reframing, and Image Playground

AFM Cloud and Cloud Pro models in Shortcuts

Third-party apps using Apple Foundation Models in Private Cloud Compute

The usage limits are per device, not per account. This means your iPhone, iPad, and Mac each have separate allowances. Apple isn’t disclosing specific limit numbers. Instead, it says that limits can vary based on the feature, request complexity, system demand, and more.

As you near your limit, you’ll see an alert within whichever feature you’re using. For example, if you are using Image Playground, a message will appear telling you that you’ve almost hit your usage limit for the day. Once you hit the limit, you’ll be prompted to wait for it to reset or upgrade your iCloud+ plan.

If you hit your limit, basic Siri requests will still work. This includes things like setting timers and alarms. Requests that require Siri to understand personal context and perform more complex, multi-step actions, however, are subject to the limits.

For example, asking Siri to find the details of an upcoming dinner reservation in your email and add them to your calendar would count toward your daily limit. 

Additionally, each device uses its own standard daily usage limit first. After that, it can tap into the additional capacity included with an eligible iCloud+ subscription:

title: Animaj Brings ‘Ozzy Fox’ Series to Disney Plus as It Charts a Path for AI in Animation
snippet: Animators using agentic AI? It’s already happening, and this is what it looks like.
fullText:
A lot has changed since I first met the team behind Animaj at Walt Disney Studios in Burbank, California, in 2025. Since teasing an upcoming project with Disney a year ago, the AI-boosted animation studio has now produced Ozzy Fox, its first combined project with the animation powerhouse.

Debuting on YouTube and Disney Junior in July and launching on streaming service Disney Plus soon, the preschool-age show features bright colors, catchy songs and a cute family of foxes. It’s drawn and animated by humans, but with an AI assist to speed things up.

In the last year, AI has become a more normalized part of the creative process, popping up everywhere from music to movies. Studios don’t shy away from saying “AI” anymore; they’re using it to make content faster while — at least in some cases — still keeping humans in jobs.

			

More from CNET

Animaj recently released FlipMove, a “pipeline” combining all of the AI models it has been developing over the past few years into a single tool for its animators to use. The studio has also created an agentic AI workflow, Animaj CEO and co-founder Sixte de Vauplane told the media during the 2026 Disney Accelerator Demo Day.

So what does agentic AI mean for animation? A bunch of agents that have access to AI tools and context about the show so they know when to use each tool, de Vauplane told me last week in Burbank. 

“We had one agent reading the notes, another one coordinating to see which kind of model we have to use,” he told me. “Here, what we wanted is to build the ultimate pipeline, CGI pipeline, for animators, for directors, that is built on a closed ecosystem of data.”

The point of AI is to reduce the time from the director’s initial notes on a storyline to the final cut being produced, he said. 

“If you can do twice the notes in the same amount of time, that means twice better in terms of quality, and that’s overall what the industry is looking for,” de Vauplane said. “This use of AI, which is artistic-centric, is really the answer we think the industry should embrace.”

Animaj animators have “full control at every frame,” de Vauplane told us. Its closed, in-house LLMs have access to context about the show, drawing style, characters and storylines so that suggestions are customized and fit in with what the team wants to achieve.

When I first met the team in 2025, they told me their technology doesn’t replace animators; it simply making their jobs less tedious. An animator sketches out each of the main poses of the characters, and then AI is used to fill in all the in-between movements of the character that could stem from each pose. An animator tweaks those poses before they’re finalized.

A demo video of the new FlipMove pipeline shows a human-drawn sketch being quickly transformed into a 3D animation, with the AI tools importing the Ozzy Fox house and characters onto the screen, and then also posing them to match the sketch.

The FlipMove AI pipeline at work, helping transform an artist’s sketch into a 3D-modeled scene.Animaj/Screenshot by CNET

The writers and animators involved still have their jobs, David Min, vice president of Disney Innovation, told me; they’re just making content a lot more quickly.

Animaj also recently published its AI manifesto online, calling slop, not AI, the enemy. AI slop is low-quality content being rapidly generated by simple prompts using AI tools online. According to Animaj, collaborative AI tools should be put in the hands of storytellers, “because rejecting AI leaves more ground to those producing slop.” 

Read more: The New Adobe Firefly AI Is All About Video Editing

Its anti-slop message followed headlines upon the release of Ozzy Fox in July that accused it of being AI slop, citing hallmarks such as unfinished backgrounds and the lack of letters and numbers on objects in the show.

The show wasn’t AI-generated; it was created and drawn by humans, with details filled in by AI tools and checked by more humans. But it raises the question: Is slop in the eye of the beholder? And how much AI is enough to call it slop?

The manifesto also argues that AI reduces the cost and speeds up the production of human-created animation, but that every hour saved should be poured back into that human work.

“AI makes more ideas affordable to try: the strange character, the unfamiliar culture, the story nobody would have greenlit,” Animaj says. “We can put them in front of families, learn what moves them and go again.”

title: Perplexity brings AI agents feature called Teammates to the Mac
snippet: This week, Perplexity has deployed its new proactive agentic AI feature called Teammates to the Mac. Perplexity Teammates were previously limited to iOS and the web. more…
fullText:
This week, Perplexity has deployed its new proactive agentic AI feature called Teammates to the Mac. Perplexity Teammates were previously limited to iOS and the web.

Perplexity Teammates now work on iOS and the Mac

Similar to Grok Bot, Perplexity Teammates are task-oriented proactive agentic AI threads that work for you without constantly being prompted. Meta Muse and ChatGPT Dots are similar, but use a single chat model rather than supporting multiple instances.

Here’s more about Perplexity Teammates:

title: Indian chip startup Bharat Semi lands $24M seed round as it eyes global AI sensor market
snippet: Bharat Semi says it has secured design wins for its AI-enabled sensor technology with companies including General Atomics.
fullText:
Bharat Semi, an Indian semiconductor startup, has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop AI-enabled image sensors, as it seeks to win customers in the United States and elsewhere.

The investment comes as the nearly five-year-old, pre-revenue startup says it has secured design wins with U.S. defense technology company General Atomics and India’s Kaynes Semicon. Its image sensors, however, remain under development, with the startup targeting its initial commercial production in 2027.

India has committed billions of dollars to build up a domestic semiconductor industry, with a hope to become an alternative manufacturing hub as U.S. companies look to diversify supply chains beyond China. The country, however, has yet to establish itself as a major chip manufacturing hub. Meanwhile, the AI boom is also giving Indian startups such as Bharat Semi an opportunity to develop specialized chips for global markets.

The New Delhi-based startup is developing programmable image sensors that combine image capture, processing, and AI capabilities on a single chip, reducing the need to send visual data to separate processors. The move could cut system costs by at least 70% compared with conventional setups that use a separate image sensor, image signal processor, and a system-on-chip, co-founder Vrinda Kapoor (pictured above, right) said in an interview.

“Our aim here is to move from sensors to sense-making solutions,” Kapoor told TechCrunch.

Kapoor, a South Park Commons fellow who earlier worked in healthcare technology, co-founded Bharat Semi in late 2021 with Vinayak Dalmia (pictured above, left), the startup’s managing director, who previously worked at McKinsey and in private equity. Its chief technology officer, Boyd Fowler, previously held the same role at image-sensor maker OmniVision.

Bharat Semi is targeting smart homes, industrial automation, surveillance, and aerospace. Without disclosing specifics, Kapoor pointed to air conditioners that could detect when a room is empty and adjust automatically and drones that could process visual information — even with the absence of more expensive computing hardware elsewhere in the system.

The startup’s first-generation sensors are already in prototyping, while its second-generation sensors, which will incorporate more advanced AI capabilities, are expected to reach the prototype stage by mid-2027, Kapoor said. Moreover, the startup plans to get those newer sensors into customers’ hands by the end of 2027.

The all-equity seed round was led by Info Edge Group, South Park Commons, and Indus Bridge Ventures, with participation from Valour Capital, Micromax, Gaingels, and individual investors. Bharat Semi, Kapoor said, plans to use the funding to expand its engineering team, complete product development, and bring its sensors to market.

Bharat Semi has about 75 employees across India and the U.S., including 10 to 12 in its American operations, which span engineering and business development in Santa Clara. The startup plans to increase its U.S. headcount to around 20 by mid-2027, Kapoor said. It has also begun hiring engineers in Europe.

“It’s a story of can we build a global technology company out of India,” Kapoor said.

In 2024, Bharat Semi announced plans for a semiconductor fabrication project in India involving a technology partnership with the U.S. Space Force. The initiative, Kapoor said, remains in development and the startup is working to identify domestic partners that would build and operate the facility.

The project is separate from Bharat Semi’s image-sensor business, Kapoor added. The startup plans to remain fabless, outsourcing chip manufacturing while focusing on semiconductor design and software. The new funding will not be used to finance the proposed fabrication facility.

The company also raised separate non-dilutive financing for new hardware as well.

Mount Thor runs macOS on Apple silicon as elastic compute instances, just as a cloud provider rents Linux VMs. Customers get on-demand fleets of Macs for work that only happens on macOS: training computer-use models in reinforcement learning environments, running secure macOS sandboxes for agents, long-running instances that let an agent work across a user’s devices under one Apple ID, and build and test farms for Apple software.

There are two ways to use its solution. With managed compute, customers pick a machine class and image, and get either a full bare-metal Mac or an isolated macOS VM with administrator access, provisioned through a web portal, a command-line tool, Kubernetes, or the API, and billed per Mac on a 24-hour basis. With customer-managed compute, an organization runs its own Macs at a Mount Thor site using its own MDM, while Mount Thor operates the facility and provides inventory by serial number, problem reporting, and event notifications.

The argument is that agents are becoming macOS users, and the demand for Apple’s platform now scales with the number of agents rather than the number of people.

“Making Apple’s operating system and silicon available at datacenter-scale is a massive untapped opportunity in AI infrastructure,” said Peter Voell, Founder and CEO of Mount Thor. “Decades of investment in accessibility and human-computer interaction make macOS the best place for agents to work and for humans to hold them accountable. And with chips like the M5 Ultra, Apple silicon is becoming a high performance, more power- and cost- efficient platform for production inference.”

The other half of its pitch is inference. The M5 Ultra Mac Studio shipped in August with up to 512GB of unified memory, which puts large open-weight models within reach of a single machine at a fraction of the power draw of a traditional GPU-based server. Mount Thor says a focus of the new funding is building what it calls the best inference lab for open-source models on Apple silicon.

“Mount Thor sits at the intersection of two important shifts: the rapidly expanding capabilities of autonomous agents and the increasing demand for compute that can support both local and cloud workloads,” said Brittany Walker, General Partner at CRV. “We’re thrilled to back Peter and the team as they make it easier to use Apple’s platforms at scale for agentic AI.”

The team comes from Cerebras, CoreWeave, Fluidstack, Nebius, OpenAI, and xAI. The company was founded this year and deployed its first data center in under six months.

Wrap up

Macs in the cloud are not new as AWS has rented Mac instances for a few years, and MacStadium has been doing so longer than AWS. Mount Thor’s pitch is that the larger customer is an AI agent that needs a Mac to do its job, and that demand grows with the number of agents rather than the number of developers.

The company says the funding will go toward expanding its compute footprint and building out the team, and that it plans to add capacity quickly to keep up with customer demand.

title: Google announces Gemini 4 Hydrogen with ‘significant leaps’ in speed, intelligence
snippet: After this week’s Carbon availability, Google today unveiled Gemini 4 Hydrogen instead of keeping the “Flash” branding. This model is billed as bringing “cutting-edge intelligence to everyone.” more…
fullText:
After this week’s Carbon availability, Google today unveiled Gemini 4 Hydrogen instead of keeping the “Flash” branding. This model is billed as bringing “cutting-edge intelligence to everyone.”

Benchmarks

Compared to Gemini 3.8 Flash (which launched in September), Hydrogen is billed as a “major standalone upgrade” with “significant leaps in both speed and intelligence.” It offers native 1 million-token input and up to 1 million output tokens. Specifically:

Hydrogen finishes “tasks 2.5 times faster at its high default setting”

“…more than [triples] Terminal-Bench 4.1 scores (57% vs. 18.2%)”

Cuts “fabricated claims by more than 5x”

Adapts “cleanly when a tool call fails or a search returns empty”

In terms of benchmarks:

“Hydrogen surpasses Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level (51 vs. 50, and reaching 54 at its highest xhigh thinking setting), while often completing tasks faster than models in its class.”

“…our partners have seen Hydrogen run 2x to 2.8x faster while reducing token usage by 12% to 23%, compared to 3.8 Flash.”

“On multi-step tasks like deep research, data analysis, and broad codebase navigation, Hydrogen ranks #5 on Agent Arena, arena.ai’s live benchmark.”

“For deep domain reasoning and analysis, it leads its class on HLE-Diamond (58.8%), ranks #1 overall on Vals Tax Agent Bench (52.3%), ties for #1 on the Vals Legal Research Bench (55.8%), and leads its class on AutomationBench-AA.”

“It outperforms other models on the new Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark (53.4%) for end-to-end agentic knowledge work over complex visual files, and on Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 (71.6%) for end-to-end professional workflows.”

Compared to 3.8 Flash, Hydrogen “reduces overreach in agentic tasks by up to 81% and under-service by up to 79%, and cuts misaligned actions and task shortcutting across tool-use and coding evaluations by 12x. When faced with impossible or blocked tasks, it is up to 2x less likely to bypass permission boundaries and achieves a 96.7% honesty rate on our internal agent honesty evaluation.”

Gemini app

In the Gemini app, Hydrogen is better at following and sticking to your tone, format, and rules, while offering clear tables and visual breakdowns. As such, “email drafts, study guides, rewrites, and documents come back ready to use on the first try.” Additionally, Hydrogen “more frequently calls the right tools (i.e., Connected Apps) and skills for the job.”

	

In the model picker, 4 Hydrogen is billed as providing “Everyday help.”

Quick answers: 3.5 Flash-Lite

Everyday help: 4 Hydrogen

Detailed research: 3.1 Pro (on AI Pro)

Code & analysis: 4 Argon

Most complex work: 4 Carbon

Free users in the Gemini app get access to Hydrogen via the “[Auto] model selection when it’s the appropriate model for the prompt.”

Google Search

Google says Hydrogen significantly upgrades Search (AI Mode) by better understanding your intent:

…you can ask your question in your natural flow of thought — even if you have multiple parts to your query, hard-to-understand typos, or highly specific requests — and Search will intelligently comprehend what you’re looking for.

Responses get more visual and will feature a wider range of relevant links. Hydrogen is the default model for AI Mode and is used for “your hardest questions” in AI Overviews.

Antigravity

	

In Google Antigravity, 4 Hydrogen has an “Extra” thinking tier alongside Low, Medium, and High. Then there’s Orchestrator: “Carbon that may offload routine steps to Hydrogen. Same Carbon-level quality, fewer tokens used.”

To help make this multi-model collaboration automatic, we’re introducing Orchestrator in Google Antigravity. Rather than using a single model from start to finish, Orchestrator dynamically switches between models like Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session.

For workflows that require parallel agents, Carbon can act as the coordinator while Hydrogen can power worker and verifier agents to build and test changes simultaneously across isolated workspaces — helping teams ship complex projects faster without driving up token costs.

Hydrogen is available in Antigravity for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers.

For developers, Hydrogen costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens.

Robert Pattinson will take on the role of James Bond in Amazon MGM’s first film in the 007 franchise. The next James Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve using a script written by Steven Knight, while Amy Pascal and David Heyman will produce.

The upcoming James Bond film will be the first from Amazon, which snapped up the rights to the franchise through its acquisition of MGM Studios in 2021. Amazon later gained creative control over the spy series from Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson in 2025 after a years-long stalemate. There hasn’t been a new James Bond film since Daniel Craig’s last installment as the spy in 2021’s No Time to Die.

Pattinson recently starred as To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen in the psychological thriller Primetime, and will appear in Villenueve’s Dune: Part Three later this year. He also played Antinous in The Odyssey. Amazon MGM will now need to find actors to play a new Bond Lady, villain, along with an M and Q, as reported by Deadline.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime,” Pattinson says in the press release. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”

Correction, November 16th: A previous version of the article said No Time to Die was released in 2015, when it was released in 2021.

title: After dodging death, battery startup Our Next Energy is now going public
snippet: Our Next Energy is the latest battery startup to go public via SPAC. Does it now have what it needs to survive in the cutthroat battery industry?
fullText:
It’s never been easy to run a battery startup in the U.S. There have been more failures than successes over the last 20 years, and whipsawing federal policy has caused more than a few battery companies to shut shop.

Not all of them die, though. Our Next Energy (ONE) had some close calls, but soon it will go public via SPAC, the company exclusively told TechCrunch.

ONE says it is valued at $600 million pre-money, and it expects the merger with Wen Acquisition Corp. will bring $400 million in gross proceeds assuming no redemptions. The combined company will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker “ONEE,” and the pro forma implied equity value is $1 billion.

Over the years, ONE has raised $483 million, according to PitchBook, and at one point was valued at $1.3 billion. It has also received tens of millions of dollars in incentives tied to investments and job creation in Michigan.

ONE is the brainchild of former Ford and Apple engineer Mujeeb Ijaz, who designed a way for electric vehicles to draw power from two batteries of different chemistries. In ONE’s first setup, it paired lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) and with a manganese-rich chemistry, which would let each chemistry play to its strengths: LFP could be used day in, day out, while the more fragile but energy-dense, manganese-rich one would work for long, infrequent road trips. An initial prototype traveled over 600 miles on a single charge. 

But the EV market didn’t take off as quickly as anticipated, and automakers wanted to buy at lower prices (usually from China). Both of those reasons helped sink ONE’s first attempt at a Series C in late 2023. The startup had to lay off a chunk of its staff, and eventually vacated its lease for a planned $1.6 billion factory in Michigan.

The rough patch led to Ijaz’s ouster as CEO in December 2023, only to have him return to the position in March 2025 after a new round of funding closed. (His brother’s investment firm co-led the round.) 

Part of the critique aimed at ONE during Ijaz’s first tenure as CEO was that the company spent too much time developing new products instead of focusing on one or two, as most startups tend to do. When Ijaz came back to the helm last year, he said that ONE would leave the automotive market and focus on grid-scale batteries.

ONE isn’t alone in pivoting away from vehicle batteries. American automakers, which had similarly rosy views of EV adoption, also bet big on battery factories and supply chains. When sales didn’t pop in the U.S. like they have in China or Europe, they had to find an outlet for that capacity, and the grid started looking like the obvious target once it started groaning under the weight of AI data centers. Both Ford and GM have announced their own energy storage products.

Many new grid-scale batteries use LFP, which is safer and cheaper than those used in most EVs in the U.S., and Ijaz saw an opportunity for ONE there as well. “We go back to the origins of LFP in this country and even to some of the factories that are in China,” he said. Indeed, just over a decade ago Ijaz led the automotive division at A123 Systems, the company that first commercialized the chemistry.

Soon, Ijaz saw other opportunities for ONE’s batteries, including defense and locomotives.

The defense play isn’t surprising. Nearly every battery company I talk with these days mentions defense, in part because it’s a market that Chinese companies can’t play in. Building an American supply chain means that a company can sell batteries at a premium, shielded as they are from Chinese competition. It’s a higher-margin market, though much smaller than EVs.

My recent conversation with Ijaz last week was the first time I’d heard a company pitch rail companies as potential customers, though. Ijaz said ONE is “finding a lot of traction in” that market. The company has built a hybrid locomotive that uses a 2.8 megawatt-hour battery, and another he calls a micro-hybrid, which uses a smaller battery to start the diesel engine faster, similar to a stop-start system on a fossil fuel car or truck. 

“Our customers are seeing a 50% improvement in diesel fuel consumption, which is a big deal,” Ijaz said.

Currently, ONE has three business lines, which could be a sign of its old culture creeping back into the picture. But Ijaz said the addition of defense and rail were driven by the bottom line: Grid-scale battery customers are also “very much like automotive customers, where they were willing to buy from China as long as the price was low enough,” he said. 

“Believe me, I would have loved to have made that grid business into the single business of the company. But the customers would look and then be taken away to a Chinese option because of the pricing, and the tariffs also leading them to that conclusion,” Ijaz said. “And so we decided that we needed a more durable market, and we looked for who in the customer base valued an American battery company.”

Today, ONE operates a pack assembly plant in Novi, Michigan, which can put together packs from cells at a rate of 3 gigawatt-hours per year. The plant uses cells from China-based and non-China-based suppliers, as well as ONE’s own cells from a smaller factory nearby, which is currently being upgraded to make 50 megawatt-hours of batteries per year.

In its investor pitch, which TechCrunch has reviewed, ONE distills its business lines into defense and rail. Drones and submarines make up the majority of what ONE sees as a $16.2 billion market. Defense-focused data centers get lumped in there, too, contributing $4.1 billion to the defense business. (That appears to be the main outlet for grid-scale batteries.) The other line, which serves the rail industry, is expected to be worth $28.2 billion.

Both markets are sizable, but they pale in comparison to the EV sector, which is worth about $73 billion today, and could grow to $200 billion by the end of the decade, according to Grand View Research. This year, ONE expects to bring in $30 million in revenue, and hopes to make double that next year. The company said it has $200 million in binding, multi-year contracts with railroads and defense contractors.

ONE hasn’t closed the door on the automotive industry, Ijaz said. “Automotive still is a race to the bottom on margins,” he said. “As time goes on, if we win an automotive contract for any purpose, we’ll take a look at it, but not at any cost.”

ONE’s pitch centers on the so-called foreign entity of concern (FEOC) restrictions: The U.S. government can’t buy batteries made in China or those made using minerals from China-controlled supply chains, so ONE will target them first. 

But it’s a pitch that many battery companies are making today. Whether investors buy into ONE’s vision will depend on if they think the company has parted with its tumultuous past and found a focus. It will need both to succeed in the increasingly cutthroat battery industry.

The result is a totally automated Apple Unified Platform currently trusted by over 45,000 organizations to make millions of Apple devices work-ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

Apple published a new security research post this week detailing Secure Exclaves, a new architecture built to handle what the company calls “ambient sensing.” The latter isn’t anything new. “Hey, Siri” has been using a version of this always-on listening technology for years. The difference now (particularly on newer devices like Apple Watch Series 12 and HomeView) is new features need far more data from your surroundings, and Apple has changed where that data gets processed.

Today, on most Apple hardware, wake-word detections run locally on-device on a smaller, low-power chip. But once it thinks it heard you say “Hey, Siri,” the main operating system gets involved to confirm and wake up the smart assistant for use. There’s nothing necessarily wrong with this process. The split second of audio is all processed locally and not sent to Apple servers.

The problem lies in Apple’s newer features that ask for a lot more from users than a wake word.

Person recognition on HomeView identifies who’s in the room by face and voice, and Siri Recap and Live Rewind need to keep a running sense of what’s been happening around you. That adds up to a constant stream of sensitive camera and mic data, and it needs a more secure way of being processed than anything Apple had before.

Much like the existing Secure Enclaves architecture for authentication, instead of passing operations to the main OS, Secure Exclaves (notice the x) run their own tiny, separate operating system. Raw data goes in and a simple “that’s Arin” or “that’s the wake word” is outputted back to the OS, everything else is thrown away. According to Apple, that data “cannot be accessed by the main operating system, apps, or Apple.”

The changes don’t stop there. In recent SB column, I mentioned how on iPhone, the green dot that appears indicating that the camera or mic is live is all software connected, not like the hardwired LED that exists on the Mac. Now on iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone Duo, and MacBook Neo, the camera and mic indicators now live inside this new exclave, meaning even a compromised OS shouldn’t be able to hide them for malicious purposes.

It’s apparent Apple is building toward this new level of ambient computing across every type of device when you read technical reports like this. Future AI-first products, like the heavily rumored AirPods Pro with inferred cameras, will most certainly built on this new Secure Exclave architecture.

Overall, this new technical post reads like Apple laying the privacy groundwork for the always-listening, always-watching products that are here and coming in the near future. It’s the privacy-first approach we’ve come to love from Apple and further demonstrates its lead on this front. I highly recommend checking it out.

fullText:
While the first HomeView units won’t reach customers until tomorrow, Apple today released a software update addressing nine security vulnerabilities. Here are the details.

Pre-order Apple HomeView

Apple HomeView gets its first system update

Apple today released HomeView Software Version 27.2 (build 24V526), which contains some of the security fixes the company included in recent updates to its other operating systems, including iOS 27.2, macOS 27.2 Golden Gate, and iPadOS 27.2.

These include a vulnerability that could allow a remote attacker to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages, as well as another that could allow a malicious Bluetooth device to pair without user interaction.

In practice, this means that users who get the device starting tomorrow are advised to update it as soon as possible, since the vulnerabilities have been publicly disclosed.

Released November 12, 2026

AirPlay

Available for: Apple HomeView

Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved state management.

CVE-2026-113963: László Várady

Bluetooth

Available for: Apple HomeView

title: Gemini 4 Carbon rolling out to Gemini app for AI Ultra, Argon remains
snippet: Following the preview at the end of last month, Google is now bringing its latest Gemini 4 Carbon model to the Gemini app. more…
fullText:
Following the preview at the end of last month, Google is now bringing its latest Gemini 4 Carbon model to the Gemini app.

AI Ultra subscribers can now access Carbon in the Gemini app, AI Mode, and Antigravity. Notably, Argon (AI Pro and up) will remain available alongside the new model.

Officially, Google says “Argon remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work, while Carbon is built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence.” Examples include “complex, multi-step coding and debugging and open-ended scientific research and discovery.”

In the model picker, 4 Argon is for “Code & analysis” and 4 Carbon is for “Most complex work.” Notably, the Gemini app has removed 3.1 Pro with this launch.

	

To showcase performance on larger, more complex projects, Google Antigravity is previewing /swarm. This turns a “single prompt into a coordinated team of agents you can track in real time.”

Developers can assign Carbon to roles that demand the deepest reasoning, like architectural design, coordination, and auditing, while pairing it with faster, lighter models across parallel isolated workspaces and adversarial verifiers that test every change.

For legal, finance, and enterprise work, Carbon is said to bring “higher-precision knowledge work, artifact generation, and data analysis.” This includes how the model will follow “strict schemas and formatting to generate polished and precise spreadsheets, presentations, and reports.”

Existing benchmarks don’t adequately capture how agents reason natively over dense files with charts, images, blueprints, schematics, and tables, so we partnered with Artificial Analysis to launch the new Multimodal Knowledge Agents (MKA) benchmark. Carbon ranks #1 while using 3X fewer tokens than the next best model across 200 tasks that test a model’s multimodal performance in agentic workflows.

Other domain highlights include:

Carbon performs exceptionally well on engineering tasks that require multi-agent collaboration like multi-package migrations, cross-subsystem root-cause investigations, and complex architectural redesigns. 

For web app development, it runs build-and-verify loops, recovers from errors, and checks both its code and the rendered UI to produce complete, working

applications. 

Stronger visual design, spatial reasoning, and attention to environmental detail also carry over to 3D game development and creative coding.

The introductory pricing for Carbon is $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens until November 30. Afterward, it will cost $4 per 1M input tokens and $20 per 1M output tokens.

Carbon is also available:

For developers: Build with the Gemini API paid tier in AI Studio and Android Studio, and if you’re a Google AI Ultra subscriber, you can try it in Google Antigravity and AI Studio.

For enterprises: Try it in Gemini for business via the API or model drop down, Google Antigravity, or specialized agents like CodeMender and AlphaEvolve.

For scientists & researchers: Apply for a chance to get access to both Argon and Carbon via Google Antigravity’s highest usage tier free of charge for 6 months (onboarded on a rolling basis), subject to eligibility, capacity, and selection.

For cybersecurity defenders: Apply to join the Fairwind Program to get access to Carbon for cyber on a rolling basis.

title: Microsoft outage saw 80% of servers fail – here’s what happened
snippet: Last week saw a truly epic outage to Microsoft 365, with a huge number of users unable to send and receive emails. The company has now admitted that at the worst point, more than 80% of its servers were unresponsive. Microsoft has now explained what went wrong, stating that the mistake that led to the failure was actually made all the way back in July without being detected … more…
fullText:
Last week saw a truly epic outage to Microsoft 365, with a huge number of users unable to send and receive emails. The company has now admitted that at the worst point, more than 80% of its servers were unresponsive.

Microsoft has now explained what went wrong, stating that the mistake that led to the failure was actually made all the way back in July without being detected …

The company said at the time that it was a technical issue and not a cyber attack, and that it was working hard to fix the problem, admitting that it was taking longer than expected. Microsoft also denied that it was related to the thousands of layoffs announced the previous month.

Users were understandably unimpressed at the scale of the outage and the time taken to fix it, although meme creators were having fun.

Microsoft’s explanation – two factors combined

	

Platform head Charles Lamanna admitted the severity of the problem.

In less than two hours, the previously unknown defect was encountered across our fleet and rendered them unresponsive. At its lowest, more than 80% of servers were unresponsive.

He said it resulted from a combination of two issues. The company maintains two independent network gateway systems, one of which failed, meaning that the remaining gateway took the full load. That wouldn’t have been a problem on its own, Microsoft stating that each one has enough capacity to handle all traffic. However, a mistake made back in July led to a cascading failure.

A latent defect caused servers to become overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions. This was due to lock contention inside an internal process which caused the machine to become unavailable. This defect was the result of a fix that was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers […]

The initial change in behavior first started deployment in July of this year. The update went through safe deployment and saturated globally over several weeks, during which time no issues were observed. For more than three months, the change was deployed worldwide without impact. Our normal load testing did not detect the latent issue because the different traffic and SKU mix used in our test labs. The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware; whereas our load testing tended to focus on our weaker hardware SKUs with fewer cores.

In other words, the update wasn’t tested under the conditions in which it was most likely to fail.

9to5Mac’s Take

While the company claims that the incident is unrelated to laying off staff and replacing them with AI systems, I find myself extremely skeptical. It seems inconceivable that a company of Microsoft’s size could make what appears to be a schoolboy error of this magnitude unless there were insufficient engineers working on the update. title: Samsung Gallery officially adds Google Photos backup, but not for all Galaxy users
snippet: Samsung has officially launched Google Photos integration in its Gallery app with backup services, and it’s also now widely rolled out for Galaxy devices. more…
fullText:
Samsung has officially launched Google Photos integration in its Gallery app with backup services, and it’s also now widely rolled out for Galaxy devices.

Samsung Gallery started rolling out support for Google Photos backup in September, but it wasn’t widely available at the time. As of this week, though, Samsung is officially announcing the feature as it is now available broadly to Galaxy users. 

“Gallery Sync” in the Samsung Gallery app replaces the previous Microsoft OneDrive integration with Google Photos, letting users sign in with their Google account of choice and use the free 15GB or paid Google One storage to back up photos and videos. This allows the Samsung Gallery app to show media backed up from another Galaxy device, but it doesn’t integrate your full Google Photos library.

At this point, Google Photos backup via Samsung Gallery should be broadly available to Galaxy owners. We’re seeing Samsung’s pop-up (pictured above) about the feature on our Galaxy Z Fold 8, with the feature fully functional beyond that. 

	

You can also access setup via Menu > Settings > “Sync photos and videos” in the Samsung Gallery app. 

Samsung requires your device to be running One UI 9 (Android 17) to access this feature, though it says that support will be “expanding to additional Galaxy devices in phases.” For the time being, though, that means the feature is a bit limited for users, as the One UI 9 rollout is still in progress.

Once media has been backed up to Google Photos, Samsung Gallery also now has a “free up space” button that can delete the local copies of your photos and videos to open up storage on your phone.

title: Google Maps can now build trip itineraries with real-time details about each stop
snippet: You could use Ask Maps to plan a holiday shopping day trip or something more complex, like a three-day road trip featuring coastal hikes and oceanfront dining.
fullText:
Google announced on Monday that it’s rolling out new Maps features that are designed to help people plan trips and everyday tasks using AI. The company is launching the ability for Maps to create trip itineraries and find appointments for users.

The new features reflect a broader shift in how tech companies are positioning AI, which is less as a tool that just answers questions and more as an assistant that can complete tasks on users’ behalf. While many companies have released AI agents to complete these tasks, Google is working to bring that approach into a service that millions of people already use every day.

Google says users can use the navigation platform’s “Ask Maps” tool to build step-by-step trip itineraries and get real-time details about their route right when they pull up directions.

Image Credits:Google

For example, you could use Ask Maps to plan a holiday shopping day trip or something more complex, like a three-day road trip featuring coastal hikes and oceanfront dining, Google says. You’ll get a day-by-day itinerary with insider tips and numbered map pins for every stop. Once you’re happy with your itinerary, you can share it with friends and family or export it to Google Docs on desktop.

When you’re ready to head out, you can use Ask Maps to reopen your itinerary or find the “itinerary” badge in your chat history. You’ll have access to real-time information, including traffic conditions, business hours, and a look at what the “vibe” is at your next stop, the company says. You could also adjust your schedule by asking Maps to do something like add a scenic viewpoint or lunch stop along your route. You can then tap any destination in your itinerary to get directions and navigate to your next stop.

Additionally, users can use Ask Maps to find beauty, pet care, auto, and home repair appointments online and call local businesses for you. For example, you could ask: “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me.” Ask Maps will then display open slots across nearby businesses.

Image Credits:Google

The new agentic calling feature arrives as tech companies continue to introduce AI agents designed to handle time-consuming tasks, such as scheduling DMV appointments and making reservations. For example, Meta’s AI agent Muse recently gained the ability to call businesses on users’ behalf.

Google also announced that you can now use Ask Maps to quickly find places on your lists by asking something like: “Which spots saved in my lists have availability for five people in the next 30 minutes?” 

The tech giant says the new updates are starting to roll out on Monday on Android and iOS. As part of the news, Google announced that Ask Maps is expanding to 30 countries across Europe, including Spain, Germany, and the U.K.

title: If you bought an iPhone Duo, have you kept or returned it? [Poll]
snippet: When Apple announced the iPhone Duo back in September, the company called it “the most transformational change to iPhone since the original,” and there’s no doubt that it generated a huge amount of excitement. But a new report suggests that for some buyers the novelty quickly wore off, and they ended up returning their devices. Is this just a handful of people, or is it more common … ? more…
fullText:
When Apple announced the iPhone Duo back in September, the company called it “the most transformational change to iPhone since the original,” and there’s no doubt that it generated a huge amount of excitement.

But a new report suggests that for some buyers the novelty quickly wore off, and they ended up returning their devices. Is this just a handful of people, or is it more common … ?

It’s been a very long time since any smartphone launch has generated quite so much buzz. Apple called it a breakthrough in iPhone design.

iPhone Duo features a breakthrough foldable design that’s beautiful, versatile, and durable, opening up possibilities that feel entirely new yet remarkably familiar […] 

“iPhone Duo is the most transformational change to iPhone since the original. With an entirely new design and intuitive experiences, it shows what’s possible when hardware and software are engineered together and redefines what it means to use a foldable phone,” said John Ternus.

Despite not really being the target market for the phone, I was still wowed by the launch video and remained incredibly impressed when I got some hands-on time with one.

Many couldn’t resist buying one despite the price – but The Verge notes that not everyone has ending up keeping the device. Apple allows you to return any product within 14 days for a full refund without having to give any reason. That window has come to an end for some of the first buyers and the site’s Alison Johnson spoke with some of those who’d decided to take advantage of it.

	

There were a few specific issues:

It’s too heavy and bulky

The outer screen is too small

The cameras aren’t as good as those on the iPhone 18 Pro

But the more fundamental reason for some is that it hasn’t really lived up to their hopes for a multifunctional device.

“If I can have an iPad in my pocket, that would be great.” So thought Ben Seligson, a content creator, photographer, and now former iPhone Duo owner […] “Usually I’d throw a YouTube video on the iPad or throw a podcast up. And then I start cooking dinner and leave my iPad in one spot, but I’d have my phone in my pocket if I got a text, or I needed to set a timer or something like that.” With the Duo, the phone was also the iPad on the counter, so a quick reply became much more of an interruption.

I’m curious as to whether this is just a small minority of buyers or a more common phenomenon. If you bought a Duo early enough to have hit the end of the return window, please take our poll to let us know whether you decided to keep it or return it – and do share your reasons in the comments (which are now back).

Oh, and the good news for anyone buying one now is that you’ll have a lot longer to make up your mind, with the extended return window for the holidays in place. You can now return anything bought today through January 8.

Software used to be a one-time purchase, but over time, with the addition of cloud storage and services, everything has become a subscription. One company even tried to make your car seat heaters a subscription. Count the subscriptions you’re paying for right now: iCloud, a password manager, a couple of streaming services, a music service, maybe a VPN, and whatever other app decided this year that it needed to be $4.99 per month for something that used to be a one-time purchase.

Everything is a service now, and a lot of people are hitting the point where one more monthly charge is one too many on principle alone. Cloud storage is the one that’s hardest to cancel, because your photos and files are in it. That’s exactly why pCloud’s Lifetime plans are worth a look this Black Friday: you pay once, and your storage is yours for life!

Pay once instead of forever

Apple gives you 5 GB of iCloud for free, which stops being enough about a week after you buy an iPhone. The irony is that they launched with 5 GB of free storage in 2011, and it’s almost laughable that it hasn’t been increased since.

After that, it’s a subscription forever. The 2 TB iCloud+ plan costs $9.99 a month, about $120 a year, for as long as you want your photos to stay where they are. pCloud’s math is different. The 2 TB Lifetime plan is a one-time payment that costs less than four years of iCloud+ at the same size, and the day you buy it is the last day you pay anything for it.

pCloud has offered lifetime plans for 9 years and now 24 million people use it, and it’s run by a Swiss company under Swiss privacy law. The “what if they go away” question is fair for any lifetime offer, and a company with that track record is the best answer you’re going to get.

If you’ve been paying for iCloud or Google Drive storage for all of your files for the last 9 years instead of using pCloud, go do the math on how much you’ve spent.

More storage for your Mac without paying Apple for it

Apple charges a lot to move from a 256 GB MacBook Air to a 512 GB one, and you can’t change your mind later with a hard drive upgrade. Storage has gotten incredibly pricey in recent years as well. pCloud Drive is your solution without breaking the bank. It’s a native Mac app that mounts your pCloud storage as a drive in Finder, so your files appear as if they’re natively on your Mac but live in the cloud until you open them. A 256 GB laptop with a 2 TB pCloud Drive behind it stops feeling small. It runs on macOS, Windows, Linux, iOS, and Android, and everything stays in sync across all of them in real time.

With pCloud Backup, backing up the folders you choose is easy and safe from a lost laptop, fire, flood, or theft. If you run a NAS at home, pCloud supports backing it up via WebDAV, Rsync, SFTP, and SCP, making it a real offsite destination for a Synology NAS, not just a simple sync folder. It would be a perfect offsite backup for small businesses, remote workers, etc.

Photos, Docs, and getting out of Google

iCloud Photos is great, but it uses storage from your iCloud storage quota, which can get expensive as Apple’s cameras get better and better and file sizes keep increasing. Every pCloud plan includes pCloud Photos, a photo gallery that organizes everything by date on a timeline, automatically tags objects and scenes, and groups shots into albums by event and person.

The pCloud mobile app backs up your camera roll automatically to free up space on your iPhone; a Memories feature resurfaces older photos, as the Photos app does; and a built-in document scanner turns receipts and paperwork into PDFs without needing a separate app. Inside the app, there is also a built-in Photo Editor with crop, rotate, brightness, contrast, highlights, shadows, and eight one-click filters, so quick fixes don’t require moving it back to Apple Photos.

pCloud Docs covers documents, spreadsheets, presentations, PDFs, text, and markdown with six built-in editors and real-time collaboration, all from the browser or the mobile app. If your household is split, with one person on Microsoft, Apple, or Google, pCloud can pull in files from Google Photos, Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive, and Facebook. That’s the easiest way I’ve seen to get everyone’s files into one place without needing to download and reupload everything.

The 3in1 Bundle: storage, passwords, and encryption for life

Files and photos aren’t the only benefit of joining the pCloud ecosystem. pCloud Pass is a password manager that works across all devices, browsers, and operating systems, with one-click login, form filling, and a generator for strong, unique passwords. Passwords are still hard, and most people are either paying monthly for a manager or reusing the same three passwords. A lifetime license solves the annoying aspects of using a dedicated password manager app or being locked into Apple’s or Google’s systems.

pCloud Encryption is client-side, zero-knowledge encryption for your most sensitive files. In plain language: files in your Crypto folder are encrypted on your Mac before they upload, and only you hold the key. pCloud can’t read them, and neither can anyone else. It’s the right place for tax returns, scans of your birth certificate, and anything else you’d rather not have sitting in a regular sync folder.

Here’s the deal you’ll want to pay the most attention to: pCloud offers an exclusive 3in1 Bundle, because it knocks out two more subscriptions at once. It’s 3 TB of Lifetime storage plus Lifetime pCloud Pass and Lifetime pCloud Encryption, and it’s the only offer that includes everything you need to ditch a vast majority of your subscriptions. Count up what this level of storage and functionality would cost you over three or four years, and you’ll see how incredible of a deal it is. If you don’t sign up today, you’ll end up regretting it in 2030.

title: I Let My Apple Watch Eavesdrop on My Conversations for 2 Weeks
snippet: I tested Apple’s new AI note-taking features in WatchOS 27.3, and now I’m more concerned about my sanity than my privacy.
fullText:
We’ve long suspected that our devices are listening to us, but what about when we invite them to do it? That’s what testing Audio Intelligence has felt like on the Apple Watch. But despite how disturbing it may sound to have your smartwatch listening and taking notes of your entire day, the reality has been a lot more mundane.

Along with the general sensor, processor, and battery upgrades, the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 introduced Audio Intelligence, a new set of features that allows the watch to listen in on conversations. 

Siri Recap generates summaries of what you’ve discussed throughout the day, while Live Rewind gives you a transcript of the last 15 seconds of audio in case you missed something.

It’s similar functionality as AI-powered recording pins like Plaud or Amazon’s Bee, but within the context of your smartwatch and without the additional cost or subscription. 

And it’s completely optional. You have to first opt-in to the features to activate them, then choose to turn the feature you want on whenever you want to start using it. Then you can leave it on all day, set it on a schedule or toggle it manually whenever you need it. If you’re like me and forget that it’s on, you get reminders that it’s still listening or to check your recaps. 

The fact that you have so much control over whether you use it and how much helped ease the creepy factor for me, but there’s still everyone else to consider.  

Beyond a barely audible chime when I double-click the Digital Crown to activate Live Rewind, there’s no way to alert others that the feature is in use and that whoever’s in earshot is inadvertently getting roped into my little experiment as well. Other wearables like smart glasses have an indicator light on the front to alert spectators when they’re recording video.

Apple has built-in privacy safeguards for the audio, how it’s processed and then deleted. I’ve broken all that down in a separate Audio Intelligence FAQ. This is about what it’s like to use it in the wild. 

I’ve been testing Audio Intelligence in the WatchOS 27.3 (and iOS) public beta for two weeks. Because this isn’t the final version (Apple says it will release publicly later this year), consider this a sneak preview. 

Live Rewind on the Apple Watch generates a transcription of what was said during the last 15 seconds.Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Live Rewind: Late to the trigger

Let’s get Live Rewind out of the way because there’s not a lot to say about it. Whether from a lack of muscle memory (or usefulness), I’ve had to go out of my way to remember the feature exists. 

I figured it’d come in handy for those “come again?” moments during conversations, but the reality is that it’s just easier to ask someone to repeat what they said than remember to double-press the Digital Crown at just the right moment. I can see it being more useful when you’re listening to a presentation or other event. 

Fifteen seconds go by a lot faster than I expect and by the time I realize something might be worth revisiting, the person has moved on with the conversation. I either missed what I intended to get or just captured the silence after. 

Siri Recap can be toggled on or off manually from the Control Center.Apple

Siri Recap: Good at meetings, bad at life

Siri Recap has been more useful, though it’s still hit-or-miss. The feature gives you high-level summaries of what it heard — it doesn’t provide a transcript to review, and it doesn’t identify who said what. It shines brightest during dedicated meetings when there’s a single conversation to follow rather than a jumble of unrelated discussions. 

One success story: I was moderating the chat for our iPhone Duo live folding test on YouTube while Matthew Murray, CNET’s lab director, answered viewer questions on the stream.

I thought I’d caught the gist of what he was saying, but the typing must’ve distracted me more than I realized because I was pleasantly surprised to learn some interesting facts that I’d missed in the Siri Recap, like “Opening a phone 20 times daily over 10 years equals 73,000 folds” or that the “machine runs approximately 22,560 cycles every 24 hours”. 

But Siri’s batting average wasn’t always that good, which made it challenging to trust the notes. During a conversation with another mom about car-pool logistics, Siri Recap pulled out action items, like who I was picking up and at what time, which I appreciated, but the information wasn’t accurate. Not only had Siri gotten the names of the kids wrong, it also had me picking up the wrong kid. Clearly, the mental load of figuring out after-school logistics is challenging even for Siri. 

Siri can’t handle the messy conversations (and TV shows)

Where things get interesting (and occasionally hilarious) is how Siri discerns what constitutes a conversation and how many topics belong in a single recap. 

Siri is generally good at accurately labeling what conversations are about: “Parent-teacher conferences,” “Car-pool logistics,” “Folding phone durability testing.” But rather than keeping them separate, as it should, it sometimes conflates two or even three completely unrelated conversations into a single recap.

I encountered bullet points summarizing a serious conversation with a friend about a medical condition alongside notes about a chaotic (albeit funny) exploding apple cider incident with my kids. The two conversations happened within the same two-hour window, but they were by no means back-to-back. 

Siri’s version:

Details about medical condition

Entire case of apple cider ruined after repeated warnings to stop shaking

No more apple cider will be brought into the house

Any remaining stickiness on the floor results in no iPad on the plane

It’s a good thing Siri Recap leaves out tone and volume cause that last bullet would’ve been in ALL CAPS.

What it did decide was worthy of a standalone recap was a discussion about wedding plans during an episode of Nobody Wants This on Netflix. To be fair, this would’ve absolutely warranted a recap if I’d been discussing my own wedding plans; however, the fact that the “conversation” happened at midnight should’ve tipped off Siri that this was a late-night binge session and not an actual conversation needing to be recapped. 

Rather than coming away better informed about the important conversations I’d had throughout the day, I came away feeling validated by the sheer chaos of it all. The constant whiplash of being pulled in a dozen different directions — bouncing between work, kids, gossip and the occasional sticky beverage crisis — was real and now immortalized (until the recap automatically expires if you don’t choose to save it). 

		

			

A case for manually enabling Siri Recap during meetings

For now, while novel, neither Siri Recap nor Live Rewind is reason enough to buy (or avoid) the Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4. They’re two of our top-rated smartwatches for their fitness, health and other smart features. Audio Intelligence is either an added bonus (it’s free) or something you can ignore altogether.

But if you do decide to venture into this brave new world of AI notetakers, my suggestion would be to use Siri Recap intentionally rather than leaving it running all day. 

Turn it on before a work meeting, a doctor’s appointment or another conversation where you might want a few notes to jog your memory later. Just make sure everyone involved knows it’s enabled and is comfortable with it, and that you’re not relying on it for crucial information. 

If the stakes are high, have a backup — whether that’s your own notes or a recording — lest you risk coming home with the wrong kid. 

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Vanessa Hand Orellana

She joined the brand first as an on-camera reporter for CNET's Spanish-language site, then moved on to the English side to host and produce some of CNET's videos and YouTube series. When she's not testing out the latest health tech, you can catch her on a hike or trail run with her family.

title: The Xiaomi 18 Pro’s rear displays support Google apps, Spotify, and custom GenAI apps
snippet: The Xiaomi 18 Pro series’ rear displays might actually be useful, after all. more…
fullText:
The Xiaomi 18 Pro series’ rear displays might actually be useful, after all.

Only a few companies have debuted phones with rear displays, and, quite frankly, most of them have been fairly useless. Xiaomi is hoping to turn all that around with the Xiaomi 18 Pro and Xiaomi 18 Pro Max’s rear display, which the company says supports Google Maps, YouTube Music, Spotify, and lots of additional apps via a nifty GenAI integration.

The news comes via GSMArena and builds on the AMA videos Xu Fei, VP & CMO of the Xiaomi Group, has been posting on X. If you haven’t seen it yet, the camera island on the back of the Xiaomi 18 Pro series looks similar to the cover screen on a flip-style foldable like the Galaxy Z Flip 8 or Motorola Razr series. It’s a full-color touchscreen and has impressively high resolution.

YouTube Music and Spotify will feature prominent play/pause and skip buttons, plus the artwork and name of the song playing. Google Maps will give you a navigation progress indicator, plus the next upcoming direction.

	

In addition to official integration, Xiaomi is letting users create their own rear display apps using a built-in GenAI app creation tool. Just describe what you want, and the onboard AI will create the app for you. It looks quite handy and should help solve the “useless” problem that prior rear displays have faced. The Xiaomi 18 Pro series will debut globally.

title: SpaceX Attempts History Friday With the First-Ever Double Catch
snippet: SpaceX is going to catch the Super Heavy rocket and the upper stage of the Starship booster, something never done before.
fullText:
A little over two years ago, SpaceX launched a Starship into orbit and then caught the Super Heavy booster when it returned to Earth, a feat it has since repeated multiple times. The company is taking the next step in rocket reusability by catching both the booster and the upper stage of its Starship on Flight 15, something never achieved before. 

SpaceX is launching Flight 15 into orbit on Friday, Nov. 13, with the 75-minute launch window opening at 5:45 p.m. ET. 

On its mission, the Starship will deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites, orbit Earth 14 times and return on Saturday. All of that is in line with most of SpaceX’s launches, of which there have been over 280 dating back to 2025. 

What makes the launch interesting is that SpaceX is attempting two things it hasn’t attempted before. 

The first is catching its latest booster, the Super Heavy V3, using Mechazilla, the informal name SpaceX gave to the launch-and-catch tower located at its facility in Boca Chica, Texas. SpaceX has caught the Super Heavy V1 successfully three times, but this is the first for the V3 rocket. The tower will use its arms like chopsticks to catch the Super Heavy V3 out of midair. 

		

			

The second is recovering both stages of the rocket. Prior Starship launches featured just the Super Heavy booster getting caught by Mechazilla while the upper stage landed in the ocean. This time around, SpaceX wants to catch the upper stage when it returns on Saturday with Mechazilla. 

How to watch Flight 15

SpaceX is streaming the flight from its X account and the company’s website. Coverage starts Friday at 5:15 p.m. ET, 30 minutes before the launch window opens. 

The stream should continue through the launch and the Super Heavy V3 catch, expected approximately 6.5 minutes after launch. The company promises “hours of live views” of Starship as it orbits Earth, offering viewers excellent views of the planet from space.

SpaceX hasn’t specified if it’s going to stream the entire mission, including the second catch when Starship returns to Earth on Saturday, Nov. 14. The expected time of arrival for that landing is 4:17 p.m. ET, assuming no delays or technical problems, which is a little more than 22 hours after launch. SpaceX streams from the same places every time, so if the company does stream it, the links above will be where to go. 

Should the launch be delayed due to weather, technical issues or something else (after all, it is Friday the 13th), SpaceX has not announced a backup launch date at this time.

The company is taking the next step in rocket reusability by catching both the booster and the upper stage of its Starship on Flight 15, something never achieved before.

SpaceX is launching Flight 15 into orbit on Friday, Nov. 13, with the 75-minute launch window opening at 5:45 p.m. ET.

snippet: Following Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia's CEO last week, Trump told reporters on Monday that he's open to seeing Huang return and that he's not certain that the woman Huang reportedly had an affair with was in fact a spy. "I think having Jensen go back- a lot of people are asking Jensen, they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn't a bad idea." Trump said he "would not mind" seeing Huang return as CEO, adding, "I threw out the name of Tim Cook, but I would say that Jensen's reinstatement- I think he learned a big lesson, I guess maybe one lesson more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that." Trump … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Stevie Bonifield

 

is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Following Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO last week, Trump told reporters on Monday that he’s open to seeing Huang return and that he’s not certain that the woman Huang reportedly had an affair with was in fact a spy.

“I think having Jensen go back– a lot of people are asking Jensen, they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea.” Trump said he “would not mind” seeing Huang return as CEO, adding, “I threw out the name of Tim Cook, but I would say that Jensen’s reinstatement– I think he learned a big lesson, I guess maybe one lesson more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that.” Trump has suggested Tim Cook step in as Nvidia’s CEO multiple times now.

When asked about reports that Alice Huang, one of the women Jensen Huang allegedly had an affair with, was a Chinese spy, the president repeatedly claimed he wasn’t sure if it were true. “I don’t know that she’s a spy at all, nobody’s proven that,” Trump said.

Trump also denied that Marco Rubio told him Alice Huang was a spy. “Usually what happens with that is that, any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy,” Trump said. “I don’t know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don’t. I don’t know that, you know, Jensen obviously has two things going. He has a family situation, which is a rough deal, and what he wants to do is sell chips.”

Trump went on to say national security “was not put at risk” by his close relationship with Jensen Huang.

Apple @ Work is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage, and protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

I’ve spent the past few weeks thinking about how Apple built up the best deal in enterprise AI. Two things happened that make me think Apple knew that all along (or maybe they didn’t and got lucky). Meta released its most capable open-weight model yet and optimized it to run on a Mac Studio. I also spent time with Osaurus, an app that runs a usable local AI model on something as small as a 16 GB Apple silicon laptop without needing a network connection. They even have two models that will run on 8 GB.

The Xserve has been dead since 2011, but its spiritual successor sits on a desk rather than in a rack.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

For the last few years, the narrative has been that Apple fell behind in AI because it didn’t have a frontier model. Siri AI got delayed, and the Apple Intelligence rollout was not great. In hindsight, I think Apple was right not to run that race, as the frontier-model business has turned into somewhat of a capital bonfire. Every frontier lab is spending billions on GPUs to be the best for a few months at a time, and the moment a model is good enough, someone else releases an open-weight version that runs on hardware you already own.

Open-weight models prove it: Muse Spark Open has 816 billion parameters, 42 billion active parameters, and a million-token context window, and Meta is giving it away. Apple didn’t build that LLM. It built the hardware that runs it. With that being said, Siri is still far behind.

Apple built the infrastructure for everything but the frontier model

Look at what Apple has shipped while everyone was waiting on them to try to compete with Anthropic or OpenAI. With Apple silicon’s unified memory, the GPU can use up to 512 GB of memory on a single Mac Studio, instead of being limited to whatever fits on a graphics card.

MLX is Apple’s machine learning framework, and it’s built specifically for the unified memory architecture of Apple silicon. If you’ve used NumPy, the API will feel familiar right away. On top of that, MLX includes higher-level packages for neural networks and optimizers, along with function transformations for automatic differentiation and graph optimization, so you can build more complex models without giving up efficiency. It also has bindings in Swift, C++, and C, which means it runs on any Apple platform.

Apple’s own Machine Learning Research post shows four M5 Ultra Mac Studios running Muse Spark Open at over 36 tokens per second, which is faster than you can read, while peaking around 300 watts per machine.

Meta’s own words on the setup:

Apple’s unified memory architecture lets the M5 Ultra’s integrated GPU use up to 512 GB per Mac Studio, so two machines can hold an entire model. And the chip’s 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth is fast enough to read the small slice each token needs. The result is two Mac Studios behave like one supercomputer with a terabyte of unified memory.

We tested a range of agentic workflows running entirely on-device, using Muse Code powered by Muse Spark Open, including shipping real iOS changes to Ice Cubes (an open-source Mastodon client) — bug fixes, new features, full build — and driving DaVinci Resolve end to end, with the model reviewing footage frame by frame to find the strongest moments and crop them vertically.

That’s the Xserve pitch, rebuilt for 2026. Apple killed the Xserve in 2011 because nobody wanted a Mac in a data center. The Mac mini came along and provided some new use cases over the years. Now, a couple of Mac Studios can host a model that would otherwise require a rack of Nvidia hardware and a power budget to match, and it does so quietly enough to sit under a desk. Apple wasn’t trying to compete with OpenAI, Anthropic, or Nvidia. It was building the infrastructure for everything except the frontier model, and it looks like that’s where the market is going. A company like MacStadium has to be loving this future as well.

It works on a 16 GB MacBook too

The Mac Studio story is the headline, but what matters most to most IT teams is at the other end of the lineup. I had Terence Pae, co-founder and CEO of Osaurus, on the Apple @ Work podcast last week. Osaurus is a free, open-source AI tool for the Mac. It helps manage local models that work offline, but it can also call a frontier model when needed. A really cool feature, when it does this, is that Osaurus runs a small local model first to find names, phone numbers, and account numbers in whatever you pasted, and swaps them for placeholders before anything goes to Claude or OpenAI.

Osaurus has no servers and no customer database. If the company went out of business tomorrow, the app would keep running until macOS broke it. Individuals use it for free. Workspaces, the paid tier, is for teams who want to share agents across their own Macs. There’s a Windows beta as well, which I think helps Apple’s case more than it hurts it. When the same app runs on both platforms, the Mac’s unified memory is the difference.

Wrap up

In talking with him, Terence mentioned he wouldn’t be surprised if a local model matches what today’s frontier models can do by this time next year. I believe him, and that’s the point. The frontier will keep moving, but good enough keeps moving too, and good enough is what most employees need most of the day. Apple spent the AI race building memory, bandwidth, and a framework instead of trying to match the frontier, and the narrative was that they were behind.

Now the most capable open-weight model in the US is optimized for the Mac.

title: Opera One for iOS adds Data Saver feature, cutting browsing data usage by up to 80%
snippet: Opera today announced that its Data Saver feature is now available on iOS, in a press release that also revealed a 20% year-over-year increase in the browser’s monthly active users. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Opera today announced that its Data Saver feature is now available on iOS, in a press release that also revealed a 20% year-over-year increase in the browser’s monthly active users. Here are the details.

Opera brings Data Saver to iOS

In a press release published today, Opera celebrated a 20% year-over-year increase in monthly active users on iOS last month, “building on its established presence in Asia and Africa while expanding its reach in the US and Europe.”

In the US alone, growth was even stronger, with monthly active users increasing 46% year over year.

In both cases, that outpaced the 16% year-over-year growth Opera reported on PC just a few days ago, when the company also announced it had surpassed 100 million monthly active users for the first time.

Behind this growth across both desktop and mobile is a broader shift in consumer expectations – users are increasingly reconsidering the default as their understanding of what a browser can do evolves.

In today’s announcement, Opera also touted the arrival of Data Saver on Opera One for iOS, which the company says can reduce browsing data usage by up to 80% by compressing images and text on its servers before they reach the user’s device.

For users, this can make a difference when travelling abroad on expensive roaming data, topping up a prepaid plan or running low on a monthly data bundle. Data Saver can also help when browsing on a weak connection.

While the press release didn’t go into detail on the privacy aspects of the feature, it did note that “the feature is optional, and users can switch it on or off and see how much data they have saved.”
