title: Tesla goes all-in on the Cybercab with upcoming €3B Berlin Gigafactory expansion
snippet: Tesla is putting Europe on its Cybercab roadmap with a €3 billion expansion of its Berlin Gigafactory.
fullText:
Just two months after putting its first Cybercabs on the road, Tesla is making a multibillion-dollar bet on mass production of the golden-hued, two-seat autonomous vehicles. 

The company announced Monday that it will spend €3 billion ($3.3 billion) to expand its Berlin gigafactory, with plans to begin building Cybercabs there in 2029. The new building in Grünheide, just east of Berlin, will be capable of producing up to 1 million vehicles per year, André Thierig, Tesla’s senior director of manufacturing for the site, wrote on LinkedIn. 

Construction is expected to begin in the first half of 2027. The expansion will make the facility the most technologically advanced of all Tesla factories, Thierig added.

Tesla has been directing more resources toward the Cybercab project, a reflection of its mission to become an AI and robotics company, rather than just an automaker. 

The company has already announced plans to cease production of the Cybertruck next year, in part to make room for Cybercab manufacturing at its factory in Austin, Texas. 

Musk doesn’t see much of a future for drive-it-yourself EVs even though demand for the Model 3 and Model Y has remained strong despite flagging U.S. sales. The company delivered more than 486,000 vehicles in the third quarter, about 6,000 more than the second quarter. Sales in Europe have been rising as EV adoption continues apace.

Musk has been far more interested in pushing the company toward fully automated driving systems that don’t require a human driver to pay attention — unlike the company’s current advanced driver assistance system, known as Full Self-Driving (Supervised).

The steering wheel-free Cybercab, which was first revealed in 2024 and launched publicly in September, is the current centerpiece of that plan. It’s notable not just for its lack of a steering wheel, pedals, and other traditional motor vehicle equipment, some of which is required under federal safety standards. (Federal regulators are currently investigating Tesla’s self-certification of the vehicle.)

Tesla’s approach to self-driving systems differs from that of competitors such as Waymo. Tesla relies solely on cameras, rather than additional other sensors such as lidar, to help its self-driving system the means to understand its environment. Camera data mimics human vision, but without sufficient training, AI models can struggle to interpret situations that additional sensor data might help clarify.

Tesla has so far taken a slow approach to its Cybercab rollout. The vehicles have been restricted from driving late at night, though Tesla has been working to extend their operating hours. In the more than two months that Cybercabs have been operating, they haven’t had any major incidents. 

That track record appears to have given Tesla enough confidence to commit  significant resources to expanding Cybercab production and availability. Tesla has about 1,307 robotaxis registered in Texas. Most are modified Model Y vehicles that are used in robotaxi services in several Texas cities. But the Cybercab numbers are growing with about 573 on roads in Austin and soon Dallas.

Now, Europe is firmly on its roadmap, too.

title: Sam Altman on Nvidia without Jensen Huang: the industry will be ‘fine’
snippet: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman acknowledged the special role Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has played in the AI boom, but ultimately thinks the industry will be “fine” without him at the helm.
fullText:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says the AI industry will be “fine” without Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the helm, even as he acknowledged the special role Huang has played in the AI boom.

Huang resigned last week from Nvidia after admitting to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Altman made his first public comments about Huang’s departure on Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley and the World event, where he also discussed topics ranging from data center pushback to recursive self-improvement.

Numerous executives and members of the AI industry have argued for Nvidia to reinstate Huang, including Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney, who were among the signatories in a public letter. Many fear that Huang’s departure may cause Nvidia to rethink the enormous financial risks it has taken that have fueled the AI boom. 

Huang is also reportedly setting up a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return. 

When asked whether he thought Huang should return to the company, Altman said: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.”

He expressed empathy for Huang’s situation, citing his own ousting from OpenAI in 2023 after board members accused him of withholding information. 

“It’s hard to imagine what the AI revolution without Jensen and the company he has built,” Altman said, adding that he sees Huang as a hero, and that “heroes have flaws.”

OpenAI and Nvidia have had a close relationship for the last decade, one that has evolved from a simple chip supplier-customer relationship into a potentially circular financing arrangement, in which Nvidia’s money helps fund purchases of its own chips. Most recently, Nvidia agreed to provide a guarantee of up to $105 billion backing OpenAI’s Ohio data center project. That’s just one of many such circular deals Nvidia has made to bankroll the AI boom while fueling demand for its own chips.

Altman said he’s not worried that the Bank of Nvidia will dry up.  

“Nvidia is, like, a behemoth of a company,” he said. “I think people still trust their guarantees very much.”

Altman acknowledged the “ambition” Huang brought to the industry, the scale of which “has been quite important.” But he didn’t go so far as to agree with the many who worry about ripple effects from Huang’s departure.

“I think there’s so much demand, and it’s so clear that AI is real, and people want to use it, and the revenues and demand are growing so strongly that I think the industry will be fine,” Altman said. “But again, I think Jensen has played this extremely special and valuable role as someone to really drive things forward with great ambition.”

title: Someone rebuilt old Android versions in your browser, and it’s an instant nostalgia hit [Gallery]
snippet: The “Android Time Machine” is a fun project that puts Android versions into your browser, giving you a quick and easy chance to play around with older versions for a quick hit of nostalgia. more…
fullText:
The “Android Time Machine” is a fun project that puts Android versions into your browser, giving you a quick and easy chance to play around with older versions for a quick hit of nostalgia.

Built on the back of AOSP builds for classic Nexus devices, “Android Time Machine” lets you quickly  access older Android versions. Specifically, Android 2.1 Eclair through Android 7.1.2 Nougat. 

The simulator runs within the shell of a matching Nexus smartphone on a desktop browser, or to fit your actual smartphone if you run it on Android. 

Versions and simulated smartphones include:

	

Android 2.1 Eclair: Nexus One

Android 2.3.6 Gingerbread: Nexus S

Android 4.0.4 Ice Cream Sandwich: Galaxy Nexus

Android 4.3 Jelly Bean: Nexus 4

Android 4.4.4 KitKat: Nexus 5

Android 5.1.1 Lollipop: Nexus 6

Android 6.0.1 Marshmallow: Nexus 5X

Android 7.1.2 Nougat: Nexus 6P

The best part here is how it works on your actual smartphone. When launched in fullscreen, it  scales to match your phone’s screen – meaning it fits even devices like the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s smaller outer display (it just shows the desktop version when open). 

Since this is running through the browser and not an actual Android build, you won’t get a perfect replication. Performance is a little hit or miss, especially with certain animations, but it works really well overall. 

The browser even simulates results from each era (oh, to go back to when Google Search wasn’t an absolute mess). Similarly, Google apps and the camera are filled with placeholders since the web app can’t access the actual camera or connect to the internet to sign into a Google account.

Seeing things like the boot animations and live wallpapers from classic Nexus phones, as well as peeking back at lost apps like Google+ and Play Music, is just such a fun little piece of nostalgia. 

“Android Time Machine” is free, and the source code is available on GitHub.

title: Google’s Intelligent Eyewear glasses from Gentle Monster are already sold out
snippet: One of the first partner brands selling Android XR glasses, “Intelligent Eyewear” as Google calls it, has already completely sold out, with Gentle Monster no longer accepting pre-orders just days after launch. more…
fullText:
One of the first partner brands selling Android XR glasses, “Intelligent Eyewear” as Google calls it, has already completely sold out, with Gentle Monster no longer accepting pre-orders just days after launch.

Google’s Gemini-powered Intelligent Eyewear lineup launched last week with collections from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, with pricing starting at $395. Just a few days later, though, over half of the lineup is sold out.

Every single Intelligent Eyewear style from Gentle Monster is currently sold out, with pre-orders no longer available. 

Warby Parker, meanwhile, still has most styles fully in stock. Some are delayed, mainly “Reid” which has the wide fit delayed as far as December 28, but others are still shipping on launch day. 

	

It’s unclear how many units were actually available, so it’s tough to say whether or not these are actually a hit yet, but it’s certainly unexpected to see a whole collection sold out this quickly. The first batch of Android XR glasses go on sale on December 10 – are you getting a pair?

title: Is bad news for Jensen Huang also bad news for the AI industry?
snippet: "Jensen is Nvidia, right? And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia."
fullText:
We didn’t see this coming. Or at least, I didn’t — a week ago, when I wrote about Nvidia’s board opening an investigation into then-CEO Jensen Huang, I assumed his job was safe.

On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Rebecca Bellan, Tim De Chant, and I discussed how Huang’s ouster went down and what it means for the larger AI economy. While Tim said he saw it coming (albeit not this quickly), Rebecca said, “I didn’t think it was going to happen at all.”

“Jensen is Nvidia, right?” she added. “And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia.”

Similarly, I marveled at how quickly Huang’s support seemed to crumble, with more scandals seeming to emerge every day. (At the same time, there are many who’d still like to see him return.) And we also took a moment to wonder what will happen to Nvidia’s investments in the larger AI ecosystem.

Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity; you can listen to the whole episode here.

Tim De Chant: I figured this was coming. I didn’t think it would happen this quickly. I thought there would be at least a few days. 

Rebecca Bellan: I didn’t think it was going to happen at all. I mean, Jensen is Nvidia, right? And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia. And we’ve got nothing but the last few years of data to show us that billionaires can do whatever the hell they want. So it was surprising to me  — it almost restored my faith in humanity, that he resigned.

But someone said to me, “If this were Elon, nothing would happen.” He would not be resigning. Nothing would be going down

Anthony Ha: Which is interesting, because I would have said, as of a week ago, or even just a few days ago, that Jensen is in the same category as Elon. I mean, no one is quite as special as Elon is, but it’s a big, incredibly successful company. Like you said — in a lot of ways, the entire AI economy is built on top of Nvidia.

And for most people, Jensen Huang is Nvidia. He’s the biggest shareholder. He has family members who work at the company, and probably most importantly, there was no succession plan in place. So this was not something that they were prepared for at all.

Rebecca: I think we should actually take a step back, because we just launched into this conversation assuming — rightly so — that our listeners will know what the heck we’re talking about.

But for those who somehow don’t, Jensen resigned on Thursday, after it came out he was having an affair with a former executive at an Nvidia customer called Megaspeed, who’s alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence. And then there was another reported affair with an Nvidia executive.

So he’s resigned. Nvidia CFO Collette Kress is jumping in as the interim CEO. She’s a longtime board member. I think it’s always interesting when a CFO steps in to be a CEO. It just means we’re going to manage expenses right now, like that’s the key. 

Anthony: I think a big part of the message is: This is not necessarily someone you should expect to be in this role for the long term. No disrespect to her, but it feels like a caretaker appointment while they figure things out.

Just to get into that backstory a little bit more, what has been really remarkable to me has been this sense that a lot of what ultimately brought Huang down, [that] stuff was at least known in intelligence circles for a while. Apparently, this report that [raises] questions, concerns about his relationship with Alice Huang is something that was circulating a year ago, or close to a year ago.

And then suddenly, everything really accelerated, Starting over the weekend, with Jensen Huang admitting to having an affair, the board saying it was investigating, but that it still had a lot of faith in him. And then this week, this other affair being reported on, and it just felt like there was all this bad news coming fairly quickly. 

But also, it wasn’t this thing that no one had known before. I guess a lot of the general public hadn’t known. So it’s this combined feeling of, “Wow, the ground kind of shifted so quickly under him,” even though the worst stuff, the possibility that somehow national security might have been threatened, is something that actually has been known by the government for nearly a year, if not more. 

Rebecca: That’s exactly right. Trump was given some warnings about Huang’s affair with someone who has ties to Chinese intelligence, potentially, and it seemed like he didn’t really mind.

I think what’s important here, though, is to note that Jensen Huang has been an advocate for loosening chip exports to China. And so this is where the crux of it is. Can anyone trust him as the CEO of this company when he’s advocating for loosening chip exports to China? Which a lot of people believe is a national security issue, because that means it will give Chinese AI companies access to our powerful chips, which will help them improve their AI, which could threaten America. 

I mean, there’s two sides of this coin. And I think, honestly, that Jensen does not need a woman to tell him that  — he just wants to sell more chips, and to anybody and everybody, and whether or not that’s good for national security or not, I think is honestly secondary to him.

Tim:  I completely agree. I think the big turning point seems to happen on November 9 — so that would have been earlier this week, Monday, when the Bloomberg report came out and suggested that Nvidia’s head attorney had some role in inquiring about the Department of Commerce’s investigation into Alice Huang.

Things seem to have accelerated in the last few days following that. And I don’t know what role exactly that report played in it, but it seems to be maybe there was a shift within government or within the board, a kind of a daunting realization of the extent to which this had spread just beyond Jensen and some affair. 

Anthony: There’s also just the question of: What does this mean for Nvidia? What does this mean for the broader AI industry? And one of the reasons those two things are very tightly connected is not just Nvidia chips themselves, but also the fact that under Jensen Huang, the company has invested very, very heavily in a number of AI startups.

People talk about the idea of an AI circular economy, and I think Nvidia has been one of the biggest players in that, in terms of both funding a lot of things, [but] also, obviously, providing the infrastructure for a lot of AI projects. So if Nvidia is going into this stage of lockdown, circle the wagons — even if it just means a small pullback, that could have really dramatic repercussions.

Rebecca: Yeah, that’s what I want to know: What happens to the Bank of Nvidia without Jensen? Is he the one leading this? 

Just to throw some numbers at you, Nvidia apparently accounts for roughly 80% of the AI GPU market. It reported $99 billion in investments and another $25 billion in commitments, plus $36 billion dollars in cloud service commitments. A lot of those include investments into CoreWeave, Nebius, OpenAI, Anthropic, major data center projects. They’ve got their fingers in literally everybody’s pie.

title: Google launches Intelligent Eyewear glasses: $395+, pre-order today, ships Dec. 10
snippet: After years of development, Google is launching its second foray into smart glasses with Intelligent Eyewear that supports Android and iOS. Pre-orders start today at Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, with the audio glasses shipping on December 10. more…
fullText:
After years of development, Google is launching its second foray into smart glasses with Intelligent Eyewear that supports Android and iOS. Pre-orders start today at Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, with the audio glasses shipping on December 10.

Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20

Intelligent Eyewear is meant to be worn all day rather than the sunglasses-heavy approach taken by others. The frames are 40-44 grams with the weight balanced evenly. 

There is a 12-megapixel ultra-wide camera for photos and videos (3K 30FPS or 1080p). You get image stabilization and HDR processing, while four microphones work to provide spatial audio capture. Google is also quite proud of its noise cancellation work.

	

There are two open-ear speakers for balanced audio and clear vocals. Control is done by a touchpad that accepts taps and swipes, or via voice commands, with Google debuting a new “Hey Gemini” hotword. 

Another way to control Intelligent Eyewear is through your Pixel Watch or Galaxy Watch, with Fitbit Air support coming next year:

Double pinch = “tap” gesture on touchpad to play/pause

Wrist turn = “swipe back” to close an experience

Palm-up double pinch = “tap and hold” to invoke Gemini (Pixel Watch only)

Each pair features a physical on/off switch so you can “wear them as regular glasses only.” On the privacy front, there is a white indicator light when you take a photo or video that gets saved to your gallery. If the light is covered or maliciously disabled, the glasses will stop recording, with Google running a hardware check when they are charging. Recording also stops when you take off the glasses.

Notably, Gemini commands that invoke the camera — like visual search or translation — will not save images or videos to your Gemini History. These visuals won’t be used to train AI models or for ad targeting. Additionally, the glasses will “automatically redact bystanders’ faces from these visuals before Gemini processes them.” 

Battery life (245mAh) is rated at nine hours on a single charge, with a fully topped-up charging case (Gentle Monster’s shown below) offering seven full charges. Power is transferred via contact pins located on the underside of the nose bridge. 

Android XR runs on the Qualcomm Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 with 2GB of RAM and 64GB of storage. Other specifications include Bluetooth 5.4, Wi-Fi 6E, and IPX4 water resistance. Samsung is responsible for engineering the hardware, while there are two eyewear brands at launch.

Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear is available in three styles and a total of 14 variations. Alden, Reid, and Wren are inspired by the brand’s “most beloved silhouettes.” Pricing starts at $395 for optical and sun styles in Pine, Saddle, and Jet Black.

The Gentle Monster Intelligent Eyewear collection features six frames in bold colors like dark red, pink, gray, and yellow, with 16 total variations. They can be paired with tinted, clear, blue, or brown lenses, with prescription options available for most designs. Pricing starts at $449 and will be available in the US and South Korea.

Intelligent Eyewear can be used for contextual visual searches, asking Gemini about your day, and having it accomplish tasks.

“…learn the story behind a street art mural you are passing by, ask for a tailored recommendation from a ‘New Arrivals’ bookshelf, or look at an event poster to check your Calendar availability on the spot.”

“…you can add items to your grocery list with a glance or check on your Uber’s status.”

“…use your glasses to catch up on your missed group chats, respond to messages, and take phone calls hands-free.”

Google Maps offers turn-by-turn directions, while there’s real-time Google Translate in over 70 languages.

Like on phones, Gemini Guided Vision “offers conversational audio descriptions to people with vision impairments.” This can be used to read fine print, identify color differences, find items, and explore unfamiliar places.

These glasses also serve as always-available headphones with support for YouTube Music, Spotify, Apple Music, and Audible. The Glasses companion app supports:

Pixel 7 and newer

Galaxy S, Galaxy S FE, Galaxy Z Fold, Flip, and Fold Ultra series running One UI 9.0 or higher

iPhone 13 Pro and up

Pre-orders for Gentle Monster and Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear start today with retail availability on December 10.

title: Google’s new Android XR glasses work with iOS, Made for iPhone certified
snippet: Google today announced Android XR audio glasses called Intelligent Eyewear that notably support iOS with Made for iPhone certification. more…
fullText:
Google today announced Android XR audio glasses called Intelligent Eyewear that notably support iOS with Made for iPhone certification.

Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20

Intelligent Eyewear is made by Samsung with frame designs from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker. There are 30 unique designs in total, and the frames weigh 40-44 grams with a 12-megapixel ultra-wide camera. 

Google’s Glasses companion client for iOS handles compute, including HDR processing, and saves images and videos (up to 90 seconds) to Apple Photos. The Made for iPhone certification comes into play for Wi-Fi Aware connectivity that allows for fast media transfers.  

	

On the privacy front, there is a blinking white indicator light when you use the camera to take pictures or record clips that are saved to your library. If the light is covered or disabled, the glasses will stop recording, with Android XR running a hardware check when charging.

Warby Parker

Gemini commands that use the camera, like visual search or translation, don’t trigger the light because those photos or videos are not saved anywhere, including Gemini History. Before that media reaches the cloud, Google redacts faces from video feeds and filters out bystander voices. This processing is done by the companion app. Additionally, that media isn’t used to train AI models or target ads. 

Other key specifications include four microphones and two open-ear speakers. Besides voice commands with the “Hey Gemini” hotword, there is a touchpad that accepts taps and swipes. A physical on/off switch lets you wear Intelligent Eyewear as regular glasses. 

On iOS, Gemini can make calls, send 1:1 messages (including via iMessage), and receive notifications.

Gentle Monster

Battery life is rated at nine hours on a single charge, while there’s a charging case that stores seven charges. Features include turn-by-turn Google Maps directions and real-time translation. On the streaming front, there’s support for Apple Music, Spotify, YouTube Music, and Audible. 

Google’s Android XR glasses require an iPhone 13 Pro or newer.

Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear is available in three frame designs, starting at $395 for optical and sun styles. Gentle Monster Intelligent Eyewear is available in the US and South Korea from $449.

Pre-orders open today with retail availability on December 10.

title: The new Apple TV has twice as much RAM as the previous model, but apps and games can’t use it
snippet: The new Apple TV 4K features an A19 chip inside with 128 GB storage and 8 GB RAM, twice the amount of memory as the previous version. Presumably, the supply crunch surrounding the memory chips is part of the reason this generation of Apple TV box jumped to a $299 price point as well. However, although the specs have been upgraded, apps and games are not actually able to use more RAM for themselves. Apps on Apple TV are limited by the operating system to 2 GB RAM each, and that cap has not changed on the fourth-generation box. more…
fullText:
The new Apple TV 4K features an A19 chip inside with 128 GB storage and 8 GB RAM, twice the amount of memory as the previous version. Presumably, the supply crunch surrounding the memory chips is part of the reason this generation of Apple TV box jumped to a $299 price point as well.

However, although the specs have been upgraded, apps and games are not actually able to use more RAM for themselves. Apps on Apple TV are limited by the operating system to 2 GB RAM each, and that cap has not changed on the fourth-generation box.

Obviously, most of the apps you run on Apple TV are streaming service clients, which generally have much smaller RAM requirements anyway. However, ostensibly, Apple markets the Apple TV as a gaming device and RAM constraints matter much more there. 

A hypothetically graphics-intensive game will easily hit the 2 GB RAM ceiling, and some fans had hoped that the new box with the new chip and double the internal memory would help here. Unfortunately, with the current tvOS software, that is not the case. 

9to5Mac independently confirmed that an Apple TV app is force-quit by the system when it allocates more than two gigabytes of memory for its process. The developer API os_proc_available_memory function also reports a 2 GB limit to the app, the same value as the third-gen Apple TV.

It is unclear whether this is an intentional policy decision, or an oversight. Nevertheless, the 2 GB limit is the status quo. Tangentially, it’s worth noting that the 128 GB of onboard storage is also not usable by a single app or game; tvOS imposes app bundle limits of about 4 gigabytes with apps able to reserve about 20 GB extra for some assets. 

Regarding the unchanged RAM limit despite doubling the internal memory on the chip, there is some speculation that Apple opted to reserve a portion of the system memory to help the performance of the Siri AI models. However, this doesn’t make too much sense to us. The most complex Siri AI features you can do on the TV offload to a connected iPhone or server backend anyway. The same Siri AI features are also available on the prior two generations of Apple TV hardware, so it doesn’t seem like RAM constraints are a meaningful factor. 

One group of users hoping for more RAM in the Apple TV was the game decomp community, which use AI to get AAA studio games running on anything from an Apple TV to an iPhone. Some of their projects have run into the 2GB tvOS limit previously, and were hoping that the new Apple TV would alleviate that. So far, that is simply not the case.

title: America’s air traffic control system couldn’t handle a single bad router
snippet: Flight statuses change from delayed to canceled at the San Diego International Airport after the FAA issued an emergency nationwide ground stop on November 13th, 2026. | Photo: Luke Johnson / The San Diego Union-Tribune via Getty Images Thirty minutes outside Atlanta, the pilot got on the intercom to announce that something was wrong. A communications issue with the Federal Aviation Administration was cascading across the country. The pilot didn't offer much detail except to say that the issue might affect gate access and connecting flights. For Amanda Khera, the timing couldn't be worse. Her family vacation to a small island off the coast of Belize had already turned into a medical scare when her 22-month-old son Rio developed a high fever and had to be rushed to a local clinic. Exhausted, they were trying to get home to Virginia Beach, Virginia, to see his pediatrician … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Thirty minutes outside Atlanta, the pilot got on the intercom to announce that something was wrong.

A communications issue with the Federal Aviation Administration was cascading across the country. The pilot didn’t offer much detail except to say that the issue might affect gate access and connecting flights.

For Amanda Khera, the timing couldn’t be worse. Her family vacation to a small island off the coast of Belize had already turned into a medical scare when her 22-month-old son Rio developed a high fever and had to be rushed to a local clinic. Exhausted, they were trying to get home to Virginia Beach, Virginia, to see his pediatrician and rest in their own bed. First, they had to connect through Atlanta.

“It was honestly pretty scary,” Khera said. “We didn’t know if the pilot was flying blind without any access to the control towers, or if planes would run into each other.”

“We didn’t know if the pilot was flying blind without any access to the control towers, or if planes would run into each other.”

— Amanda Khera

She had every right to be scared. She didn’t know what was going on in the cockpit or on the ground. She had no idea that pilots are trained to follow strict procedures that minimize safety risks during major air traffic control outages. All she knew was that several recent incidents, including a midair collision over Reagan National Airport in 2025 that killed 67 people, have called into question the safety of America’s skies. So she spent the rest of the descent looking out the window for nearby aircraft.

Her flight landed safely. But she deplaned into a terminal frozen in place. More than 600 flights out of Atlanta, including their connection to Norfolk, had been canceled. And no one knew when they would be able to take off because every flight across the United States had been grounded.

On Friday, November 13, the nation’s air traffic control system began to fail. Around 3:15PM ET, pilots and air traffic controllers in the Midwest started reporting difficulty communicating with each other over the radio.

“We’re 11,000 [feet] over Grand Rapids airport, about nine miles to the west,” said the pilot of Allegiant Flight 547, his transmission already becoming garbled. “Unable to get… contact… approach on any [frequency].”

Four minutes later, controllers at Quad Cities Airport in Moline, Illinois, reported similar issues across the region.

“We’re dealing with some communication issues on a larger scale than we initially anticipated,” said one. “It sounds like Chicago Approach is going ATC zero, so it might be worse than we initially thought. We thought it was just here.”

With communication outages spreading around the country, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop at 3:54PM ET “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” From that moment on, no airplanes were allowed to take off in US airspace.

The sudden halt surprised both pilots and controllers.

“Just a heads up, we went in a national ground stop,” said a controller in Seattle.

“Are you saying national as in Reagan National,” asked one United pilot, “or national in the whole country?”

“Across all en route facilities, they’re having communication issues.”

Like so many of the safety incidents that have plagued the air traffic control system over the last few years, this latest failure began with a fragile and outdated piece of FAA infrastructure. In this case, according to the agency, the faulty system was the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure, or FTI.

Built by defense giant L3Harris in the early 2000s, FTI is the data backbone of the entire air traffic control system. It links more than 4,400 aviation facilities and carries the voice and radar data controllers rely on to keep planes separated, bridging the gap between the FAA’s legacy phone-based transmission systems and modern Internet Protocol-based ones.

FTI is scheduled to be replaced in 2028. Until then, L3Harris must make incremental upgrades to keep FTI operational.

“We’re dealing with some communication issues on a larger scale than we initially anticipated.”

— Air traffic controller

One of these upgrades accidentally brought down the entire system, according to The Wall Street Journal. Early in the day, L3Harris contractors replaced an old wired telephone switch with a new fiber data router at the FAA radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas. Once activated, however, the router began to flood the network with hundreds of connection attempts every second.

This may have added enough extra load to the system to degrade the whole network’s performance, according to I-Hong Hou, professor of electrical and computer engineering at Texas A&M University.

Hou explained that telecom networks break pieces of information — radio transmissions or radar coordinates, for example — into data packets small enough to be transmitted over the network and reassembled at the other end.

“When the network is degraded, it may start to lose a small portion of packets,” Hou says. “Since you need all packets to reassemble the data feed, just dropping one out of 10 packets may cause your feed to completely stop.”

Most modern communications apps are built to compensate for packet loss. FaceTime, for example, will blur the video or switch to audio-only to preserve the connection.

Air traffic control doesn’t have that luxury.

“Many NAS [National Air Space] applications … require a highly reliable synchronization source with exceptional stability,” according to FAA technical documentation, which warns that instability may cause widespread failure of critical systems.

FAA technicians believe the El Dorado router’s repeated connection attempts created enough instability within the FTI to cut off radio and radar feeds to 17 of the FAA’s 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers and several Terminal Radar Approach Controls.

“We sometimes call this a cascading failure, meaning that one failed device can cause nearby devices to fail, and so on,” Hou says.

“We sometimes call this a cascading failure, meaning that one failed device can cause nearby devices to fail, and so on.”

— I-Hong Hou, professor of electrical and computer engineering at Texas A&M University

L3Harris’s contractors isolated the malfunctioning router and another one at a nearby radar facility in Amarillo, Texas. Once those two routers were taken offline, the network began to stabilize once again.

Four and a half hours later, at 8:15PM ET, the FAA lifted the ground stop. It was the nation’s longest since 9/11, spurring airlines to cancel more than 13,000 flights and delay more than 25,000 more through the weekend, according to FlightAware. And more than 1.5 million passengers were stranded.

Faulty technology created the crisis. The FAA’s hamfisted attempts to reassure the public that everything was okay made the situation worse.

For six hours after the ground stop began, the FAA did not provide any public updates except for a terse, 31-word press release and a single X post. Finally, at 11:30PM ET, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin held a press conference to explain the day’s events.

Instead of providing clarity, however, they issued confusing and sometimes even contradictory statements. Mullin opened the conference with a joke (“Welcome to Friday the 13th, right?”) before confidently declaring that “there is no cyberattack.” Instead, he appeared to blame the outage on the FAA’s modernization project.

“As Secretary Duffy and FAA was going in and putting patches into the system, they were putting new equipment and new technology, and that new equipment and technology was just overwhelming the older system,” said Mullin.

Mullin’s remark appeared to surprise Duffy, who looked at the ground and shook his head. Mullin later walked the statement back after a reporter’s follow-up question, admitting that “there’s nothing completely certain right now.”

Duffy offered more details but did not exactly give a straight answer. “Our switches and routers actually got overloaded with data, and they went down,” he said. “I shouldn’t say they went down. They started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers.”

“I don’t want to rule out nefarious activity,” he later added.

“This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like,” Mullin concluded. “We are built to handle crisis like this.”

A follow-up press conference on Saturday afternoon was equally bizarre. It started with piercing audio feedback produced by a faulty microphone, which interrupted Duffy right after he introduced Rebecca Guy, the FAA’s acting chief technology officer.

After a four-minute delay, Duffy continued with the briefing. He floated the potential that contractor “incompetence” had caused the outage. And he demanded that Congress allocate billions more dollars to the FAA so it could complete its modernization efforts — calling its existing $12.5 billion modernization budget a “partial payment.”

The conferences only flamed online rumors that the outage was caused by a cyberattack or a rogue AI tied to the September rollout of the FAA’s new SMART system. (So far, no evidence has emerged for either.)

The problem was compounded by an administration already struggling to command public trust. When cabinet officials offered shifting, improvised explanations from the podium, millions of anxious travelers — and even prominent allies — simply refused to take the government at its word.

“Until proven otherwise, not some presser by our government, I firmly believe this was a DDOS attack,” former National Security Adviser Mike Flynn wrote on X. “This is what was being described by two smart cabinet officials who clearly did not understand the technical nature of what happened.”

Khera and her family didn’t know about the political gamesmanship behind the outage — and frankly, they didn’t care. She just wanted to get out of Atlanta on something other than an airplane.

After a night in one of the last available hotel rooms in Atlanta, she and her family rented a car and drove the nine hours back to Virginia Beach. They made it home late Saturday night.

Because of the FAA’s mishaps, they don’t plan to fly again anytime soon.

“We’ve had enough of planes,” she said. “It will take a couple months and more explanations from the FAA to make sure something like this or worse doesn’t happen again.”

Correction, November 16th: L3Harris contractors replaced an old wired telephone switch with a new fiber data router at the FAA radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, not a wireless one. This story has been updated to reflect that fact.

title: Zoox robotaxis are now on the Uber app in Las Vegas
snippet: This is the first time Amazon-owned Zoox has partnered with a ride-hailing platform.
fullText:
Zoox robotaxis are officially available through the Uber app in Las Vegas, marking the Amazon-owned autonomous vehicle company’s first partnership with a third-party ride-hailing platform.

The launch on Monday is a milestone for both companies. Uber gets to add another partner to its app as part of its broader strategy to become the primary purveyor of autonomous vehicle technology in North America, Europe, and the Middle East. Uber has partnered with more than 30 companies developing autonomous vehicle technology for sidewalk delivery robots, self-driving cars, robotaxis, and drones — though not all of those have turned into commercial deployments yet.

For Zoox, the partnership and launch gives it access to more potential customers who might otherwise not try its robotaxi, a needed boost as it trails market leaders Tesla and Waymo.

The partnership is expected to extend beyond Las Vegas. Zoox will begin initial robotaxi operations in Los Angeles this year (introducing the robotaxi and opening rides to Zoox employees, family, and friends), but commercial service will not begin until 2027. Rides will be available via the Uber app next year as well. 

For now, all eyes are on Las Vegas, Zoox’s first commercial market and a city where Uber has ambitious robotaxi plans.

The two companies also announced a multi-year partnership with MGM Resorts International: they’re rideshare and robotaxi partners for MGM Resorts properties in Las Vegas. Uber and Zoox said they’ll work with MGM Resorts to improve pickup and drop-off locations, along with signage to help riders navigate sprawling MGM properties and find the robotaxis.

Earlier this year, the Nevada Transportation Authority unanimously approved a permit that allowed Uber to deploy up to 1,000 robotaxis in Clark County — home to Las Vegas — through its partnerships with Hyundai subsidiary Motional and Zoox.

Zoox’s addition to the Uber app comes with some initial limitations. Customers won’t be able to select a Zoox robotaxi — at least initially. Instead, people who request an UberX, Uber Comfort, Uber Electric, Uber Comfort Electric, or Wait & Save ride may be matched with one of Zoox’s custom-built robotaxis once they hail a ride. Customers can increase their chances of getting a Zoox robotaxi by opting for autonomous rides through “ride preferences” in the Uber app’s settings.

Uber plans to introduce a dedicated autonomous option in its app as “availability and reliability improve,” Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said during the company’s third-quarter earnings call in November. 

“Las Vegas will become the first U.S. city where riders can access two fully driverless partners through the Uber app,” he said on the call. “We will begin with limited fleets and expand supply over the coming months, with plans to introduce a dedicated autonomous option in our app.” 

The plan to offer a dedicated autonomous option marks a shift in Uber’s approach to robotaxis, including its partnership with Waymo. 

That exclusive partnership, which matches Waymo robotaxis with Uber riders in Austin and Atlanta, will end in January 2028. Waymo plans to offer its rides directly through its own smartphone app as it does in other cities. TechCrunch previously confirmed with Uber that it still plans to host Waymo robotaxis on its app for as long as the two companies agree. 

And unlike its partnership with other AV developers, Uber told TechCrunch that it will not provide maintenance and other services for Zoox in the Las Vegas market.

title: Google and Adobe partner to add app integration in Google Drive, Gemini
snippet: Google Drive will soon prompt users to switch to Adobe Acrobat while viewing PDFs, and Gemini will get a few new tricks powered by the company’s creative suite. more…
fullText:
Google Drive will soon prompt users to switch to Adobe Acrobat while viewing PDFs, and Gemini will get a few new tricks powered by the company’s creative suite.

The pipeline from PDFs opened in Google Drive and Gmail to Adobe Acrobat is notoriously strained. That goes for any PDF viewer, but as soon as certain tools are necessary, a large number of users rely on Adobe’s products to edit and store documents.

Google announced plans to ease the process. According to a press release today, Google will be adding a “direct pathway” from Google Drive and Gmail in Adobe Acrobat. Acrobat will be suggested to users within the services, which will likely act as a quick transfer sort of feature. It doesn’t seem to indicate users will see any Adobe PDF editing tools within Google Drive. Google Drive has notoriously fallen short in this regard.

The partnership announcement also means Gemini will get access to some of Adobe’s creative tools. Further detail isn’t clear, but that includes Gemini, Gemini Enterprise, and Google AI Mode in Search. It sounds like the integration will allow users to edit or manage PDFs and other files straight from Google’s AI interfaces.

	

It’s not just PDFs and Google Drive; Adobe’s Photoshop gets a shout, too. Expected sometimes in the future, we may see  more powerful image editing powered by Gemini within Adobe Photoshop, as opposed to the current models and limitations within. Gemini Nano Banana models are currently in use, but AI generation and editing could go further with a more focused effort. Google says the push “could enable near-real-time edits,” but there’s no concrete timeline set for when we could see that.

title: iOS 27.3 adds new setting to bypass website cookie popups (eventually)
snippet: iOS 27.3 is currently in beta and packed with new features, including a ‘Global Privacy Control’ setting in Safari that could someday put an end to cookie consent pop-ups. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.3 is currently in beta and packed with new features, including a ‘Global Privacy Control’ setting in Safari that could someday put an end to cookie consent pop-ups.

Safari has new ‘Global Privacy Control’ setting in iOS 27.3 for automatic cookie opt-outs

Apple has several big changes coming to Safari in iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3. The browser is adding Vertical Tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode, and new Siri AI powers.

But iOS 27.3 has another Safari feature that’s hidden away in Settings: a new ‘Global Privacy Control’ option.

Inside Settings ⇾ Apps ⇾ Safari ⇾ Advanced you’ll find the ‘Use Global Privacy Control’ setting. Apple describes it this way:

Safari can ask websites to not sell or share your data. This may cause some websites to not function properly or work at all.

The beta also links to a support document where users can find more information, but it’s currently a broken link. The document will likely be published on iOS 27.3’s release day.

	

As noted by Nick Heer on his site Pixel Envy, this Global Privacy Control setting is “effectively a replacement for Do Not Track with legal muscle that should permit you to indicate your tracking preference one time and then, theoretically, never again see a cookie consent banner.”

Ultimately though, the dream of automatically declining cookie consents has a long road to reality. Websites have to add support for Global Privacy Control (which some have already done, but most haven’t). And GPC currently only has legal muscle in five US states.

That said, the addition of a Global Privacy Control setting in iOS 27.3 is a good start. And hopefully it means that in a few years, many Safari users don’t need to see cookie consent popups anymore.

snippet: Apple will soon be adding a video podcasts section to Apple TV, which will also be available in the Apple TV app on other devices like smart TVs. fullText:
Apple will soon be adding a video podcasts section to Apple TV, which will also be available in the Apple TV app on other devices like smart TVs. That means it will come to more than a billion devices in total.

Access to the video podcasts will be free, with no requirement for an Apple TV subscription. Testing begins today, with the full rollout promised “soon” …

Apple shared the news with The New York Times.

On Monday, Apple will add a video podcasts section to Apple TV, initially just for testing with developers. They will soon be free to all users […] Apple also plans to increase the number of video podcasts on its regular Podcasts app.

The company says the move will benefit creators and listeners alike.

“We want podcasts to be available wherever people want to enjoy them — the small screens, big screens,” said Oliver Schusser, a vice president at Apple who oversees services including podcasts, television and music. “It’s really about discovery and helping the creators to reach a new audience. We didn’t approach this in a way that would financially benefit us.”

While podcasts began as audio only, it’s become increasingly common in recent years for them to be released as video also. This expands the reach to video platforms like YouTube, Hulu, and Netflix. Creators have welcomed Apple’s latest move, even if some are a little sad about what it says about the medium.

“It’s so helpful that people can go on their phones, they see a clip on Instagram, TikTok or Twitter and open the Apple app and now watch it on video,” he said. “People are already on their iPhones and they’re used to watching videos on their phones so it was the next logical step” […]

“Everything is TV now, which is a little bit heartbreaking for a lifelong audio person to say,” Ms. Martin of NPR said.

No date has yet been announced for the public rollout.

fullText:
Google is launching a new AI trip-planning feature for Maps that allows the app to create custom itineraries for you and provide real-time details about each stop. The update, which is rolling out to the Gemini-powered Ask Maps chatbot inside the app, lets you plan a one-day outing or a trip spanning several days.

As an example, Google says you can use Ask Maps to plan a day trip for holiday shopping, or have it create a schedule for a three-day road trip with stops for coastal hikes and oceanfront dining. From there, Ask Maps will generate a day-by-day schedule with a list of stops, while also showing your route and numbered pins for each location on the map. You can share the itinerary with friends or family members, as well as export it to Google Docs on desktop.

You can ask Maps to show your trip schedule before you leave, or select the “itinerary” badge in your chat history. Along with directions, Google Maps will display real-time information about traffic, a location’s hours, and more. You can also view “know before you go” details about parking, car charging, weather conditions, potential delays, and tolls during your trip.

In addition to trip planning, you can now use Ask Maps to find specific beauty, pet care, auto, and home repair appointments, and have it call the locations for you. You can also use Ask Maps to find saved places on your list by asking something like, “Which spots on saved in my lists have availability for five people in the next 30 minutes?”

Google is expanding Ask Maps to over 30 countries in Europe, including Spain, Germany, and the UK. Trip-planning and saved list search is rolling out to the more than 200 countries where Ask Maps is available, while “know before you go” tips and appointment-finding are launching in the US to start.

fullText:
Good morning. Today I’m trying desperately not to buy Sony’s new nostalgia-bait headphones, reeling from how emotionally invested I was in Spider-Man: Brand New Day (yes, I know I’m late), trying to figure out what a “private, agentic notebook” is, and slowly coming around to the idea of the New York Times owning Letterboxd.

Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

The relationship between Samsung and Google has, over the years, waxed and waned depending on their respective interdependence. Samsung is Android’s physical emissary, powering a plurality of all its handsets globally. But Google, and in particular its services, is the glue that holds Samsung’s smartphone experience together. 

	

The back and forth is over a decade old; back in early 2014, Samsung shipped a refreshed magazine-style skin with its Galaxy tablets that eschewed many of the design tenets Google had been pushing its partners to adhere to. Not only was Samsung willfully defying its most important partner, but it made a point of barely mentioning Android during its press conferences.

Around the same time, it transitioned its smartwatches from Android Wear to Tizen and began shipping duplicative apps on its devices (many of which persist to this day). The goal was to distance itself from Google as much as possible.

While we don’t know exactly what happened behind closed doors, we saw the outcome quite clearly: Magazine UX lasted one product cycle, and the two companies signed a 10-year cross-license patent deal, which may have helped Samsung prevent any future lawsuits with Apple. Google then sold Motorola to Lenovo, clearing the way for Samsung to continue building its burgeoning hardware business on the back of Google’s mobile ecosystem.

Since then, the two companies have grown even closer. In 2021, they co-announced a new Wear OS along with an overarching wearables partnership that has since grown to include Android XR as well. And Google is still the default search engine for Samsung devices, despite reported inroads made by Microsoft in 2023 to convince the Korean giant to switch to a ChatGPT-powered version of Bing Search. (Samsung’s ongoing relationship with Microsoft, which bundles its Office suite on most Galaxy devices, could be seen as a point of leverage for negotiations with Google, too.)

This brings us to today, and to AI. Samsung was among the first companies to adopt Google’s full suite of Gemini Intelligence products, and its phones often get new AI features before anyone else. But like a decade ago, when Samsung shipped Bixby to kind-of-sort-of compete with Google Assistant, it still wants to offer its own services alongside Google’s.

So a rumor that Samsung may launch a paid Galaxy AI Premium subscription next year for $5/month piqued my interest for the same reason Magazine UX did 12 years ago. Galaxy AI features today are a blend of first-party and third-party capabilities, but none of them are especially useful, particularly when compared to Google’s own Android equivalents powered by Gemini Intelligence. Now Bar and Now Brief, two heavily promoted features in Samsung’s marketing, are wildly disappointing.

At I/O this past May, Google announced Spark, an agent that goes out and performs actions on your behalf. And while it’s since been somewhat eclipsed by more capable mobile options like Meta’s Muse, it’s obvious that Google is working on a follow-up that will perform functions both on the phone and inside apps.

That’s exactly what Samsung is rumored to be working on with Bixby Action, a spiritual successor to its namesake that, when it debuted, prioritized on-device tasks like turning on Wi-Fi over web-based actions Google Assistant did better.

According to leaks from SamMobile, Galaxy AI Premium will offer agentic upgrades for phone users to “create commands triggers and system routines for daily tasks” or “automate routine daily tasks using Galaxy AI.” Gen Video will reportedly “convert static photos into dynamic video clips,” while a new Daily Briefing likely does what it says on the tin.

Will Samsung users see enough value in this hodgepodge of features paywalled only because they use a surfeit of compute? And what models will power them on the backend?

Right now, Google is in the enviable position of being able to offer its AI at three distinct layers: the model itself, which is invisible to the user; the OS level, which can promulgate Gemini across every Android phone that runs Google services; and the hardware level, where Pixel lets it specialize and optimize.

Samsung, not particularly known for its software prowess, will likely need to step gingerly around Google’s AI shadow while also justifying the cost to shore up its much-needed services revenue. Based on this leaked roadmap, though, I’m not confident it will work out.

Instead, Samsung may want to acquire one of the many up-and-coming AI agent startups whose valuations are rising more quickly than their user bases. While Muse and OpenAI’s Dots have taken up most of the recent conversation, I’ve been using Hark, Town, and Instinct pretty regularly for a month or so and could see them being brought in-house by Samsung and offered either as standalone products or customized for Galaxy devices. As Google is doing with its own AI plans, Samsung could provide Galaxy users a year of free service, after which they would be expected to pay. 

Samsung doesn’t have a great history of building software, but many of its acquisitions, from SmartThings to Viv Labs (which became “next-gen” Bixby) to LoopPay (which became Samsung Pay) to Whisk (which became Samsung Food), have proven successful. Given the current urgent state of mobile AI, I’d forgo the hodgepodge and bring in some outside expertise.

title: Apple Maps in iOS 27 has hidden new feature I’ve been loving
snippet: iOS 27 gave Apple Maps a handful of new features, and my favorite is one that keeps offering fresh updates every week: Local Lists. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 gave Apple Maps a handful of new features, and my favorite is one that keeps offering fresh updates every week: Local Lists.

Apple Maps adds weekly-updated ‘Local Lists’ feature for trending restaurants and more

Apple Maps has long offered a ‘Guides’ feature where you can browse curated collections of places worth checking out. Sometimes they’re created by Apple’s editorial team, other times by celebrities or in conjunction with current events.

But in iOS 27, there’s a new feature—Local Lists—that’s sort of an extension of Guides, but it gets updated weekly with the latest trending places.

Here’s how Apple describes it, via Apple Newsroom:

With Local Lists, Apple Maps users in the U.S. can find the perfect spot for meeting friends, dining, and more. Using intelligent insights from what’s trending, Maps surfaces locally relevant collections of places — from trending restaurants to great spots to take kids — so it’s easy for users to find what they are looking for. All insights are derived with privacy in mind and never tied to individual users.

I’ve always enjoyed browsing Guides in Maps to help find new places. But Local Lists are a great expansion of the idea, especially since they’re updated all the time. I’m always up for trying a new trending restaurant, and now Maps makes it easy to stay on top of what’s new.

How to find Local Lists in the iOS 27 Maps app

Even if you’ve been using iOS 27 for months, there’s a good chance you’ve never seen Local Lists. That’s because they’re pretty hidden. 

To find the feature, tap into the search field in Maps and scroll down to see a new ‘Trending Restaurants’ section. On my iPhone 18 Pro, by default this section gets hidden behind the keyboard, so you have to first scroll and dismiss the keyboard to see it.

Trending Restaurants are ranked from 1-20. The search screen shows only a handful, but you can tap to view the full list. For example, if you open the ‘Trending Restaurants in New York’ list, you’ll see 20 places worth checking out.

How does a restaurant make the list? Per the in-app explanation, the list contains “Restaurants climbing in popularity this week, based on what people view, share, and interact with on Apple Maps.”

	

Since these Trending Restaurants lists update weekly, Apple says you’ll want to save any places you plan to visit. There’s a convenient + button next to each listing.

It’s unclear exactly how many different parts of the US have localized lists in iOS 27. But if you poke around and find the full collection of Local Lists, there are 1,021 total—so you’ll probably have one in your area.

You can browse all available lists by opening a Trending Restaurants list then tapping where you see the Apple logo and ‘Local Lists’ near the text that says when it was last updated.

title: Meta issues a high-priority update to prevent some glasses from getting ‘too warm’ when wet [U]
snippet: The latest Meta Glasses (not Ray-Ban or Oakley-branded) may temporarily overheat if they get too wet, but a software patch is here to help prevent that. more…
fullText:
The latest Meta Glasses (not Ray-Ban or Oakley-branded) may temporarily overheat if they get too wet, but a software patch is here to help prevent that.

Folks using Meta Glasses in the Adventurer, Fury, Starfire, Nova, or Capri styles should open the Meta AI app on their smartphones and get their glasses updated as soon as possible. Meta sent out an email to all Glasses owners noting that the company has “an important software update” related to performance when “excessive moisture or sweat” enters the device. Meta specifically says this issue does not affect Ray-Ban or Oakley-branded Meta glasses.

Meta sent out an email to all Meta Glasses owners with the tagline “Action required,” noting that this could be a potentially serious issue:

“We’ve implemented a software update to fix a rare issue that caused a small number of Meta Glasses to get too warm when moisture entered the device. It works similarly to a phone shutting off automatically when it needs to cool down. If people experience this, they can contact Meta Customer Service for a replacement.”

– A Meta Spokesperson

The new software update brings your glasses to version 130, which includes a special software hook that shuts them down if they were to get too warm. Meta told me that the temperature for this threshold is quite low, and that the glasses shut off to prevent any potential issues. The company was very specific about the wording in the statement, carefully using the word “warm” instead of “hot,” so as to avoid the stigma that comes with that term on wearable technology.

	

While I haven’t seen any specific reports of Meta’s newest glasses models overheating, there are plenty of Reddit threads citing overheating issues on Ray-Ban Meta glasses over the years. Ironically, the one post I found related to sweat-related overheating was from a year ago on Ray-Ban Meta glasses, which this software update does not address.

To update your glasses, follow these steps:

Open the Meta AI app.

Tap the Glasses icon in the top right.

Select the settings icon for your Meta Glasses model.

Select your paired glasses model from the list.

Tap Updates.

Tap the Check button and tap Install when it appears, or turn on automatic updates.

Meta Glasses were launched this summer as a budget-minded alternative to the company’s Ray-Ban and Oakley-branded AI glasses. The glasses start at $299, which is substantially cheaper than the $379 Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 or the $449 Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 options. Meta Glasses come in several different styles, including special LISA and Kylie-branded ones, and offer identical functionality to the more expensive Ray-Ban or Oakley options.

title: Google Antigravity adds ‘Knowledge Work’ interface for non-coding work
snippet: Following last week’s big update, Google Antigravity is rolling out a “Knowledge Work” user experience. more…
fullText:
Following last week’s big update, Google Antigravity is rolling out a “Knowledge Work” user experience. 

Antigravity launched with a coding focus, but Google has seen how people, including employees internally, are using it for “far more than code.”

Alongside software engineering, more and more daily sessions center on deep research, data analysis, drafting documents and presentations, prototyping designs, and automating everyday workflows.

The company shared that “tens of thousands of Googlers outside software engineering (across sales, finance, legal, product, design, research, marketing, and operations) now rely on Antigravity every week alongside engineers to get their work done.”

As such, Google Antigravity now has an optimized Knowledge Work experience that joins the existing Software Engineering interface. The underlying Antigravity agent is unchanged “with full access to frontier models, local files, plugins, skills, rules, custom agents, and MCP servers.” 

	

When Knowledge Work is enabled, you’ll see the following UI changes:

Area

Software Engineering

Knowledge Work

Projects and folders

Prompts for Local or New worktree mode on Git repos; shows Git branch pickers, GitHub controls, and Open in IDE; forks can target a new worktree.

Runs directly in your project’s folders without worktree or Git branch prompts; hides GitHub and Open in IDE controls; forks stay in the current folder (Fork conversation in this folder).

Conversation and approvals

Keeps expandable Worked for tool groups, inline code diffs, line counts, and subagent cards in the thread; permission prompts include raw command-rule editors.

Shows a live progress line while the agent works that clears once the response finishes, keeping focus on replies and artifacts; permission prompts present plain-language summaries.

Side panel and Overview panel

Overview includes Review, Files, Terminal, and Extensions rows, a Customize Sections menu, and sections for Subagents, Background Tasks, Goals, Documents, Artifacts, Links, Modified Files, and Uploads.

Overview stays hidden until the conversation produces output, omits Review, Terminal, and Customize Sections, labels the Files sidebar tree Folders, and focuses on Documents, Artifacts, Links, Uploads, and Background Tasks.

Customizations (Installed tab)

Lists installed Plugins, Skills & Rules, Custom Agents, and MCP Servers.

Lists installed Plugins only (installed skills, rules, custom agents, and MCP tools remain active in the background).

Settings

Displays developer subsections (Terminal, Workspaces, and Labs) and detailed permission rules directly.

Tucks advanced permission rules and developer subsections behind Advanced Settings in Settings > General and project settings, and hides the Appearance > Conversation Steps toggle and code syntax preview.

To enable, go to Settings > General > Interface Layout. On first launch, there’s a new onboarding flow.

Google launches Intelligent Eyewear glasses: $395+, pre-order today, ships Dec. 10

Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear Prices

For Warby Parker, we’ll focus on the “Reid” model, the rectangular lens shape. Like the rest of the catalog, these start at $395 with non-prescription lenses, either clear or tinted. Single-vision Rx: +$100

Readers (magnification): +$100

Progressives: +$330

Anti-fatigue: +$100

Anti-reflective: +$35

Blue light filtering: +$50

Notably, there’s a further upcharge for adding prescription lenses to sunglasses versus standard clear glasses.

The prices for Google’s first collection of Android XR glasses are not cheap, especially when you consider the add-ons. title: Mazama Energy has a solution for geothermal’s biggest drilling problem
snippet: Khosla-backed Mazama Energy has developed a new way to supercool its geothermal drill bits, letting it drill faster and deeper in a quest to bring down the cost of electricity.
fullText:
Success in geothermal energy is guided by two basic goals — drill fast and drill deep. Hit both targets, and geothermal startups have a good chance at being cheaper than nearly every other source on the electrical grid. 

But while the goals might be straightforward, they’re anything but easy. Drilling fast generates heat, which damages equipment, and so does drilling deep.

Those two foes are what led Mazama Energy to develop a new technology, called Carbon Chill, that uses carbon dioxide to cool the drill bit and bring cuttings to the surface. The technology will not only let the company drill deeper, but also faster. The startup gave TechCrunch an exclusive look at Carbon Chill.

“Our rate of penetration increased 20% over the already very high rates we were achieving,” Sriram Vasantharajan, co-founder and CEO of Mazama Energy, told TechCrunch.

Speed has other advantages in geothermal. Drilling represents about 25% to 30% of the total cost of building a power plant, so reducing drill time can bring costs down significantly.

If geothermal startups succeed in drilling faster and cheaper, they stand to help reshape the grid in the 2030s. Hyperscalers are already planning the facilities that will enter operation at the end of the decade. 

Mazama has been working on the problem for years now. In October 2025, the Khosla-backed startup said it had drilled a well in Oregon that reached 629˚ F (331˚ C), and a more recent well has surpassed 700˚ F, Vasantharajan said. In September, the startup raised $135 million in a round led by Centaurus Capital and Doerr Capital.

Mazama hopes that its new carbon dioxide-based cooling technology will help it prove that geothermal energy from super-hot rock is a viable contender in the electricity market.

Already companies like Google and Meta have started to explore the use of geothermal energy, in part because the potential is enormous: A report from the National Laboratory of the Rockies said that geothermal could generate between 26.5 to 57 terawatts of electricity in the U.S. alone. If just 10% of the conservative estimate were developed, it would more than double the U.S.’s peak generating capacity. 

Geothermal experts have identified super-hot rock — in which temperatures exceed 752˚ F (400˚ C) — as a promising way to improve the performance of individual wells. At those temperatures, water turns “supercritical,” a gaseous-like liquid state which carries five to 10 times more energy than water from traditional geothermal wells. By harvesting more energy from each well, developers have to drill fewer of them, bringing costs down.

Accessing that heat can be challenging for traditional drilling methods. Most geothermal drillers use “mud” — a combination of water and other compounds to keep the bit cool and clear cuttings from the borehole. But mud can only bring temperatures down so much. Eventually, they become so hot that electronics in the drill bit, which help keep it on course, start to fail.

High temperature-rated electronics exist, but they’d be cost prohibitive, Vasantharajan said.

Instead of mud, Mazama injects liquid carbon dioxide down the center of its drill string. As it travels deeper, it gets heated by the rock around it, which turns it supercritical, too. Then, just before it reaches the drill head, Mazama has it flow through a valve that looks a lot like a rocket nozzle. As the gas expands, it escapes through the cone-shaped nozzle and rapidly cools, absorbing heat from the electronics and the drill bit. 

“I look at [carbon dioxide cooling] as a binary,” he said. “Without such technologies, I am, today, not able to drill these horizontal wells at super-hot rock temperatures.”

That capital injection will help Mazama drill more wells deeper. By next year, Vasantharajan said his company hopes to complete a single well that’s capable of generating up to 15 megawatts of electricity. 

“What was just a dream or a quest, I can tell you with confidence is now a promise,” he said. “We see a path towards this commercial super-hot rock geothermal.”

Tim De Chant is a senior climate reporter at TechCrunch. He has written for a wide range of publications, including Wired magazine, the Chicago Tribune, Ars Technica, The Wire China, and NOVA Next, where he was founding editor. 

De Chant is also a lecturer in MIT’s Graduate Program in Science Writing, and he was awarded a Knight Science Journalism Fellowship at MIT in 2018, during which time he studied climate technologies and explored new business models for journalism. He received his PhD in environmental science, policy, and management from the University of California, Berkeley, and his BA degree in environmental studies, English, and biology from St. Olaf College.

title: Jensen Huang resigns as CEO of Nvidia
snippet: Jensen Huang has resigned as the CEO of Nvidia following recent reports of extramarital affairs, including one involving a woman suspected of spying for China. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Jensen Huang has resigned as the CEO of Nvidia following recent reports of extramarital affairs, including one involving a woman suspected of spying for China. Here are the details.

Nvidia appoints interim CEO as search for permanent replacement begins

In late October, The New York Times reported on Jensen Huang’s “close relationship” with Alice Huang, a former managing director at Singapore-based Megaspeed, whom US intelligence officials reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset suspected of passing information to Beijing.

According to subsequent reports, Chinese intelligence allegedly recruited her to gather information about Jensen Huang and influence his position on selling advanced AI chips to Chinese companies. China disputes the espionage allegations, dismissing them as groundless speculation intended to smear the country.

That said, while Nvidia previously denied any impropriety in their relationship, Huang admitted last weekend to having an extramarital affair in a message to employees, saying, “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did.” He did not mention Alice Huang directly.

In the following days, concerns grew over the potential national security implications of the relationship, in addition to Nvidia seeing its stock plummet.

And while Huang remained CEO as Nvidia’s board commissioned an independent investigation into the allegations, The New York Times reported on Wednesday that he had a second extramarital affair, this time with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him.

In the hours that followed, The Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia’s board was preparing to meet to decide Huang’s future. Soon after, Semafor reported that some board members favored Nvidia CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO, while other reports suggested that Huang’s daughter, Madison Huang, could eventually succeed him. Madison Huang works at Nvidia as senior director of product marketing.

Semafor also named Apple’s chief hardware officer, Johny Srouji, as a potential successor, while Bloomberg reported that Nvidia had hired an outside firm to identify candidates.

Now, Nvidia has officially announced that Huang “has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately.”

The company confirmed that Kress has been appointed interim CEO, while retaining her current responsibilities, until a permanent successor is named. The company is considering both internal and external candidates.

Nvidia also announced that Harvey C. Jones, a longtime technology executive and venture investor, has been appointed the company’s first-ever board chair.

In a statement, Jones said the board has “full confidence in Colette and the leadership team,” adding that Nvidia expects its operations, customer commitments, and product roadmap to continue without interruption.

	

Nvidia did not directly address the allegations surrounding Huang in its announcement, instead thanking him for his contributions to the company over the past 33 years.

Following the Times’ Wednesday report, Nvidia shares plunged in after-hours trading, erasing the day’s 2.9% gain after two consecutive sessions of losses.

The stock continued to fall following today’s announcement, dropping more than 10% at the time of writing from Wednesday’s closing price of $173.73, bringing its total decline to approximately 35% from its October 6 record close.

How Nvidia’s stock will behave when the market opens today and in the days that follow is anyone’s guess, especially with the company scheduled to report its quarterly earnings next Tuesday, November 17.
